But then he says the structure “grows,” and suddenly we are in biology, not architecture: the church is not a finished monument to be maintained but a living thing, still becoming what it is meant to be, still being fitted together by the Spirit (he will develop this in 4:15–16). He needs both images: the building gives the church its solidity, the body its vitality. With only the first it turns rigid and institutional; with only the second, shapeless and rootless. Rooted and growing, fixed and alive.

“Joined together” is sunarmologoumenē, a word found only in Ephesians (again in 4:16) — precise fitting, each stone set exactly where it belongs and bearing on what is next to it. There are no spare stones in this building, no redundant members in this body (cf. 1 Pet. 2:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes on five words holding God’s whole ambition for his people: a dwelling place for God. Not a place where people come to find him, but where he himself takes up residence — actually, personally at home. And it raises a wonder: why would the God who fills all things (1:23) want a dwelling place?

Because he has always longed to dwell among his people. It is a thread running the length of Scripture. He walked with Adam in the garden (Gen. 3:8); when sin shattered that, he told Israel to build the Tabernacle “that I may dwell in their midst” (Exod. 25:8) — the word shakan gives us Shekinah, his settling, glorious presence. That glory filled the Tabernacle and later Solomon’s Temple so completely that no one could stand to minister (Exod. 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11). He did not merely receive honour there; he moved in. Then came the catastrophe: because of Israel’s idolatry, Ezekiel watched the glory depart the Temple, slowly, reluctantly (Ezek. 10–11) — and the deepest wound was not the Babylonian army but the presence leaving before it came. Yet Ezekiel was given a promise: the glory would return (Ezek. 43:1–5; and the city’s new name, “The Lord is there,” 48:35).

And it returned in a form no one expected. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” — skēnoō, tabernacled, pitched his tent — “and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The Shekinah came back, not to a building of stone but to a body. Then at Pentecost the Spirit descended not on a temple but on people, tongues of fire resting on each one (Acts 2:3) — God moving in again, now into his people. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). It is “by the Spirit” because the Spirit is the mode of God’s indwelling in this age — the living presence of God within the community that gathers, prays, suffers, and loves.

And here is the staggering thing: God wanted a dwelling place, and he chose not a cathedral or a holy mountain but broken, forgiven, still-being-sanctified people. The ordinary congregation on a Sunday morning, with all its unfinished edges, is the dwelling place of the living God — not when it becomes worthy enough, but now. John Stott called the meeting of these last verses one of the most breathtaking things in all of Paul: that the cosmic temple God is building and the local congregation of ordinary believers are the same thing. You are not a spectator. You are a stone in the dwelling place of God on earth (cf. Rev. 21:3).

3.title: The Mystery of Christ and the Fullness of God
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles — <sup>2</sup>assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, <sup>3</sup>how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. <sup>4</sup>When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, <sup>5</sup>which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. <sup>6</sup>This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. <sup>7</sup>Of this gospel I was made a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given me by the working of his power. <sup>8</sup>To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, <sup>9</sup>and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things, <sup>10</sup>so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. <sup>11</sup>This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, <sup>12</sup>in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him. <sup>13</sup>So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory. <sup>14</sup>For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, <sup>15</sup>from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, <sup>16</sup>that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, <sup>17</sup>so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith — that you, being rooted and grounded in love, <sup>18</sup>may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, <sup>19</sup>and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <sup>20</sup>Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <sup>21</sup>to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul begins to pray and then stops himself. "For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—" and then the sentence breaks off, swallowed by a parenthesis that doesn't resolve until v.14. He cannot proceed to the prayer without first explaining the stewardship that has brought him to prison — because the mystery he has been entrusted to proclaim is itself the reason for the prayer, and the prayer only makes sense in light of the mystery. Paul is constitutionally unable to speak of anything without grounding it in the gospel.

The mystery he describes is one of the most world-altering disclosures in all of Scripture. "The Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel" (v.6). In the Old Testament, the Gentiles were at the periphery of God's purposes — they could be blessed through Israel, they could join themselves to Israel, but they were not Israel. Now the secret is out: the wall was always meant to come down. The distinction was always meant to be temporary, a pedagogy pointing toward its own dissolution. In Christ, there are no second-class citizens of the Kingdom, no Gentiles-in-the-anteroom. Fellow heirs. Fellow members. Fellow partakers. The same body. The same promise.

And the disclosure of this mystery has dimensions that exceed the merely human. "Through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (v.10). The angels are watching the church. The principalities and powers — the spiritual intelligences that inhabit the heavenly realm — are learning the wisdom of God by observing the community of the redeemed. The church is God's cosmic classroom. When a Jew and a Gentile, a slave and a free person, a man and a woman sit together at the Lord's table — the universe sees something it could not have deduced by any other means: the manifold, many-coloured, inexhaustible wisdom of a God who makes all things new.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

The concept of "mystery" (mysterion) in Pauline theology is not something puzzling or obscure. It is a technical term for a secret previously hidden in God that has now been disclosed in the gospel. The mystery of Christ — the inclusion of the Gentiles as co-heirs — was not absent from the Old Testament, but it was not fully clear. It was there in the Abrahamic promise ("in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," Genesis 12:3), in the prophets (Isaiah 49:6; 60:3), in the Psalms (Psalm 87; 96:3). But the full disclosure awaited the coming of Christ and the apostolic proclamation of the gospel.

This "already hidden, now revealed" pattern is the structure of all biblical revelation. The Old Testament is full of types, shadows, and partial disclosures that only become fully visible in the light of Christ. This is why the Reformers insisted on the unity of the two Testaments — they are one revelation progressively unfolding, not two contradictory religions. And it is why reading the Old Testament through the lens of Christ is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of its own internal logic. The mystery of the Gentiles was always there; the church is now living in the age of its full disclosure.

Paul's description of himself as "the very least of all the saints" (v.8) has been the theme of Reformed meditation on gospel humility. The man who had been the church's most zealous persecutor, who had dragged men and women to prison and consented to their deaths, now counts himself the least worthy recipient of the grace he proclaims. This is not false modesty; it is the grammar of genuine encounter with grace. The closer you are to Christ, the more clearly you see how far you fall short — and the more marvellous it becomes that grace extends even to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul describes his ministry as the proclamation of "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (v.8). The Greek word for "unsearchable" (anexichniastos) means literally "untraceable" — riches so vast that you cannot find their boundary, cannot trace their perimeter, cannot reach their end. To the Ephesian church, surrounded by the very traceable riches of Artemis and the mystery cults — gods who could be appeased, blessing that could be earned, secrets that could be unlocked for a price — Paul announces something of a different order entirely. The riches of Christ are boundless. They cannot be exhausted. The more you receive, the more remains to be given. No mystery religion could offer this.

Now: Paul is in prison when he writes this, and he explicitly tells the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings (v.13). The apostle who has been entrusted with the most glorious news in the universe is sitting in a Roman cell when he writes it. This is the pattern of the gospel: its glory travels in the most unlikely vessels. The imprisoned apostle, the persecuted church, the minority community that the world dismisses — these are the means through which the manifold wisdom of God is made known. When the church is most visibly weak, it is often doing its most significant cosmic work. The angels are watching — and what they see is the wisdom of God displayed in jars of clay.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul begins to pray — “for this reason” picks up the cosmic reconciliation of chapter 2 — and immediately interrupts himself with a parenthesis that will not close until v. 13. He cannot speak of the mystery without first explaining his own role in it. But before the explanation, he names himself plainly: “I, Paul.” And “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” — not Rome’s prisoner, though he sits in chains. His imprisonment is not defeat but vocation, the cost of proclaiming the mystery to the Gentiles. He belongs entirely to Christ, and it is on their behalf that he wears these chains. Calvin: “The very chains of Paul are more to be glorified than all the triumphs of kings.”

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard of the stewardship of God's grace that was given to me for you, how the mystery was made known to me by revelation,
verseByVerse.commentary: “Stewardship” (oikonomia) — the same word used in 1:10 for God’s own plan. Paul’s apostleship is not self-appointed; it is a trust of divine grace entrusted to him for others. Everything he has received comes as gift and responsibility. The mystery was “made known to me by revelation” — not by study or tradition but by direct divine disclosure, supremely on the Damascus road (Gal. 1:12). Paul has written about this before; his readers know the outline. What follows is not new information but a deeper sounding of what they already hold.

verseByVerse.quote: as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word mystērion runs through Ephesians seven times, and it is easy to hear it as something obscure or mystical — a truth kept deliberately dark. That is the opposite of Paul’s meaning. In the Greco-Roman world a mystērion was the secret rite of a mystery cult, knowledge reserved for the initiated and sworn from outsiders. Paul borrows the word and empties it: his mystery is not kept secret but proclaimed, not for a select few but for all nations, not hidden in ritual but written down and read aloud.

For Paul a mystery is precisely this: a truth hidden in previous ages and now disclosed by God — “hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints” (Col. 1:26; Rom. 16:25–26). The hiddenness was God’s timing, not the truth’s unimportance. So whenever Paul says “mystery,” hear: something God was keeping until the right moment has now been brought into the open.

And the hiddenness was real. The Old Testament prophets spoke of blessing coming to the nations, of a servant who would be a light to the Gentiles (Isa. 42:6; 49:6). But the precise shape — that Jew and Gentile would become one body, fellow heirs of equal standing, the dividing wall entirely gone — was not yet visible. Present in seed, anticipated in promise, but veiled. Calling it a mystery honours both the continuity with the old and the genuine newness of what is now made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: The mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In v.3 Paul said simply “the mystery”; now he names it — the mystery of Christ. Not something puzzling about Christ, but the mystery that centres on him and could only be disclosed through him. He is both its content and its key. In Ephesians it has two dimensions: the cosmic — God’s purpose to unite all things under one head (1:9–10); and the ecclesial — that Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, fellow partakers in Christ (v.6). Not Gentiles brought under the Jewish covenant, not two peoples on improved terms, but one body of equal standing.

And it is finally the mystery of a person. Everything Paul will say about the church and the purposes of God flows from who Christ is and what he did in his body on the cross. The mystery is not an idea Christ illustrates; it is a reality Christ is — put most personally in Col. 1:27, “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” The risen Christ actually indwells his people, Gentiles included without qualification, and in doing so makes something the world had never seen.

“Which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed” — not absent from the Old Testament, but not yet fully visible there. The prophets saw it in outline and searched to understand what the Spirit was pointing at (1 Pet. 1:10–12); what they could not see was the precise shape — one body, the wall down, equal access to the Father — which had to await the cross, the resurrection, and the apostolic witness (cf. Col. 1:26–27).

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the same promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three “fellow-” compounds in the Greek (sugklēronomos, sussōma, summetocha) hammer the same note: equal standing. Fellow heirs — the same inheritance. The same body — not a parallel one. Partakers of the same promise. And it comes “through the gospel”: the proclaimed word is the instrument of inclusion, not circumcision or Torah.

The promise is the Abrahamic one — that in his seed all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3) — and the seed is Christ, in whom Gentiles become Abraham’s heirs (Gal. 3:16, 29). Exactly how they share is where covenant theology and dispensationalism read Paul differently. Covenant theologians (Calvin, Hodge, Vos) hear Gentile believers sharing fully and equally in the one covenant of grace made with Abraham and fulfilled in Christ — grafted into the one olive tree (Rom. 11:17), the “mystery” being that this full inclusion was not clearly seen before. Dispensationalists (Ryrie, Walvoord, MacArthur) hold a careful Israel–church distinction: the church shares the spiritual blessings flowing from those promises, while specific promises to ethnic Israel await a future fulfilment, and the “mystery” is the church age itself, unpredicted in the Old Testament.

But whatever their difference on the shape of the promise, both affirm what Paul states plainly: Gentile believers have genuine, full, equal standing before God in this age. There is no second-class membership in the body of Christ — not a guest at another’s table, but a full member of the household. Both traditions have produced believers who love the same Lord and trust the same gospel. The differences are real; the common ground is deeper (cf. Gal. 3:29; Rom. 11:17; Eph. 2:12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The very least of all the saints” — Paul coins a new comparative of “least” (elachistoteros), pushing below what Greek grammar allows. Not false modesty: he hunted and imprisoned the very people he now serves (1 Cor. 15:9; Acts 8:3). The man who called himself least was entrusted to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ. That is not irony; it is the gospel on display.

“Riches” (ploutos) is one of Paul’s favourite words in this letter — the riches of grace (1:7; 2:7), of glory (1:18), and now of Christ himself. He keeps returning to it because no word is large enough, and piling it up is the nearest he can get to abundance beyond all categories. And the riches of Christ are not an asset he distributes at arm’s length; they are him — forgiveness, adoption, reconciliation, union with him, the Spirit, the inheritance, and deepest of all, his own person: “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Phil. 3:8; Col. 2:3). To have him is to have the source of every other richness.

And they are “unsearchable” — anexichniastos, untraceable, like a path through a forest whose footprints simply stop; you cannot map it or find its end (the same word describes God’s ways in Rom. 11:33). The riches of Christ do not deplete as more people draw on them. No theology exhausts them, no lifetime of preaching depletes them, no eternity reaches their bottom. This is what Paul was sent to preach — not a moral code but the inexhaustible wealth of a person who gives himself to those with nothing to offer in return.

verseByVerse.quote: and to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery hidden for ages in God, who created all things,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names his second commission: not only to preach the riches of Christ but “to bring to light for everyone what is the plan of the mystery” — to illuminate what God has been doing so that those who hear can see it. The “plan” is oikonomia, the ordered administration of a household run by a purposeful manager: nothing random, nothing wasted, everything moving toward an intended end. The one new humanity, the church — these are not a contingency or a revision but exactly what God was managing toward from the beginning.

It was “hidden for ages” — and the hiddenness was deliberate, God revealing as much as each stage of history could bear and holding the fullness back until the fullness of time (Gal. 4:4). More than that, it was hidden “in God” himself — held within his own eternal counsel, accessible to no creature until he chose to disclose it. No angel knew it; no searching could have found it, because it was hidden not in the world but in the one who stands behind the world. “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:7–8). It was revealed not by discovery but by disclosure.

And Paul adds, pointedly, that this is the God “who created all things.” Not filler. The God who hid the plan is the Maker of the world in which it was hidden — so his concealment was total and sovereign; no creature can search the mind of its Maker without consent. And it signals scope: the God who created all things has been working to unite all things in Christ (1:10). Creation and redemption have the same Author and the same horizon; what was hidden in the Creator is now unveiled for the whole creation (cf. Col. 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is one of the most breathtaking purpose statements in the New Testament: God’s plan was not merely to save individuals but, through the church, to display his wisdom to the watching spiritual realm. The church is not only the beneficiary of the mystery; it is the medium of its announcement to the cosmos.

The word for that wisdom, polupoikilos (“manifold”), is found only here — many-coloured, richly varied, the word used of embroidered cloth. God’s wisdom is not a single colour but a spectrum, seen in full only across its full canvas. And the canvas is the church: the community where the impossible has happened, where former enemies — Jew and Gentile, once divided by the deepest boundary the world knew — now share one table, one bread, one Lord. No diplomacy or moral effort ever dissolved that division; the only explanation is what God did in Christ. The wisdom shows in the method too: he chose the weak and foolish things to shame the strong (1 Cor. 1:27–28), a crucified Messiah as cornerstone, a persecutor as chief missionary, forgiven sinners as the display of his glory.

And the audience is “the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” — spiritual powers who appear four times in this letter (1:21; 2:2; 3:10; 6:12), unusually prominent because Ephesus was the centre of magic in the ancient world (Acts 19:19), a city gripped by fear of named powers that had to be appeased. The display is not for their benefit but a declaration — like a conquering king parading his triumph. Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Col. 2:15), and the church is the ongoing public proclamation of that victory. Every time former strangers call the same God Father, God is saying to every power in the cosmos: look what my wisdom has done — you could not have predicted it, could not prevent it, and cannot undo it. They exist now as defeated, subordinate, watching creatures.

verseByVerse.quote: This was according to the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cosmic sermon preached through the church flows from God’s “eternal purpose” — literally the purpose of the ages — planned before time and realised in Christ Jesus our Lord. And on that eternal foundation Paul builds a startling claim: in Christ “we have boldness and access with confidence.” He said it already in 2:18, and now he says it again, stronger — because it needed saying twice.

His readers had come out of a world of spiritual dread: the pagan gods were capricious and unapproachable, managed by ritual; and even the true God was so holy that access ran through a priest, a sacrifice, and elaborate purification — the high priest entering once a year, with blood not his own. Against all of that, Paul says every believer now has bold, direct approach to the Father. The word for boldness, parrēsia, was the citizen’s right to speak freely before a ruler — openly, without fear, as a free person in full standing. Applied to prayer, it means you do not approach God with hedged, carefully managed requests hoping not to overstep; you speak freely, and bring the real grief and the honest confusion (“let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace,” Heb. 4:16).

And prosagōgē — access — is the right of approach into a king’s presence, granted by one with the standing to bring you in. Your introducer is Christ himself, whose welcome at the throne is permanent; being in him, you share that welcome, and it does not fluctuate with your performance on a given day. Paul presses the point because the tendency is always to shrink back — and he is writing from prison. What I suffer in chains, he means, does not change what you have in Christ: your access rests on an eternal purpose formed before time and realised in the risen Lord, and nothing in history can close the door he has opened (cf. Heb. 10:19–22; Rom. 5:2).

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask you not to lose heart over what I am suffering for you, which is your glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has been in prison for years, and he knows the people he loves are anxious about it. So before the great prayer he pauses: do not lose heart over my sufferings. And then a phrase that stops you — they “are your glory.”

Picture a father who works night shifts to put his children through university. The nights are hard and thankless; but one day they graduate, futures open before them, and you could say those long nights were their glory — his cost became their inheritance. Paul is in chains because he preached the gospel to the Gentiles — he took the message God gave him for the nations and actually delivered it, at personal cost, until the authorities ran out of patience. The Ephesians are believers because Paul preached; Paul is a prisoner because he preached. His suffering purchased their place. So when they look at him in chains, they are not looking at a man abandoned by God but at the cost of their own salvation written into a human life.

And there is a deeper point: suffering inside God’s plan is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The Ephesians were tempted to read the imprisonment as proof that the gospel was fragile; Paul flips it — my chains are not an interruption of the plan but part of it, the same logic as the cross, where the death that looked like the end was the turning point. As Tim Keller put it, the suffering of the servant is often the very means by which the mission advances. Paul does not say despite my sufferings you have the gospel; he says through them you have your glory. Look again: this is not evidence against God’s faithfulness but of it (cf. Col. 1:24; 2 Cor. 4:17; Phil. 1:12–14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul falls to his knees. He began to pray in v.1 and was swept away by the parenthesis of his own apostolic calling. Now, in v.14, he returns to his knees — and what follows is the most doxologically charged prayer in the New Testament. Four requests of escalating grandeur, each one building on the last, until the whole structure reaches a summit it cannot contain and erupts into one of the greatest doxologies ever written. The prayer is a mountain, and at its peak the clouds part.

He prays first for inner strengthening by the Spirit in the inner person — the deep, hidden, interior part of the human being where the real life is lived. He prays then for Christ to dwell in the heart by faith — not merely to visit, but to take up permanent residence, to be at home there. He prays third for the comprehension of something incomprehensible: the breadth and length and height and depth of the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge. Four dimensions — suggesting something that cannot be measured in any direction, a love that exceeds every capacity to contain or categorise it. And then, the goal that gathers all of this up: "that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." The finite vessel of the human soul invited to receive the infinite fullness of the divine life.

The doxology that follows (vv.20–21) is the most expansive statement of God's power to answer prayer in all of Scripture: He is able to do "far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us." The Greek accumulates superlatives: "above all," "abundantly above all," "exceeding abundantly above all" — language stacking on language, because language cannot contain what Paul wants to say about the inexhaustible capacity of God to exceed every prayer and every imagination. We always pray too small. God always answers beyond the asking. The prayer ends where the letter began: to Him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Indwelling Christ and the Fullness of God

The prayer of Ephesians 3:14–21 reveals the goal of the Christian life with startling clarity: not moral improvement, not doctrinal accuracy, not even evangelistic fruitfulness — but the fullness of God. "Filled with all the fullness of God" (v.19) is a goal so vast it cannot be reached in a lifetime, which is precisely the point. The Christian life is not a project with a completion date; it is a journey into an infinity that perpetually exceeds the traveller. John Calvin commented that Paul "had no measure in his desires" for the Ephesians — he asked for the infinite, because the infinite is what God offers.

The means of this fullness is the indwelling of Christ. "That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (v.17) — the verb "dwell" (katoikein) means to settle, to take up permanent residence, as opposed to merely passing through. This is not the occasional visitation of religious experience; it is the abiding presence of the living Christ in the interior life of the believer. The Reformers consistently emphasized that union with Christ — not merely forgiveness, not merely a changed record before God, but genuine, living union with the risen Lord — is the foundation of the entire Christian life. It is from this union that everything else flows: assurance, holiness, prayer, service, suffering, joy.

The doxology of vv.20–21 is also a theology of prayer. It teaches us that God is not limited by the smallness of our asking. The greatness of our petitions cannot exhaust His capacity to answer; the boldness of our faith cannot outrun His willingness to give. The God to whom we pray is the God who can do more than we can imagine asking — and the power by which He does it is "at work within us." It is the same resurrection power of Ephesians 1:19–20. Our prayers are small; His answers are not required to match them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The mystery religions of Ephesus promised spiritual fullness — union with the divine, access to hidden power — through initiation, through ritual, through the gradual ascent of the initiated. The costs were significant: financial, social, sometimes physical. And the fullness promised was always partial, always provisional, always requiring the next level of initiation. Paul prays for his readers to receive a fullness that no mystery religion could offer and no initiation could achieve: the fullness of God Himself, freely given, received through faith, sustained by the Spirit. The contrast with what Ephesus was selling could not have been more pointed.

Now: "Far more abundantly than all we ask or think" — this phrase has stood as one of the great encouragements of Christian prayer across the centuries. When we pray small, God answers large. When we cannot find words, the Spirit intercedes. When the situation seems beyond recovery, we serve the God who raises the dead. The doxology of Ephesians 3 is not merely a liturgical flourish; it is a declaration of the character of the God to whom we pray. He exceeds our prayers not because He is indifferent to them but because He is inexhaustibly generous. Every time this doxology is spoken in corporate worship, the church is reminding itself — and the watching powers — of who their God is.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul “bows his knees” — a posture of urgency and submission. In Jewish practice prayer was normally offered standing; kneeling was reserved for moments of intensity. This is no routine intercession; he is pressing in, prostrate before the Father for people he loves.

“From whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” — there is a wordplay English loses: patēr (Father), patria (family), sharing one root. Paul’s point is that the very concept of family — belonging, being named, having a household you are bound to — exists because there is an original Father from whom it all derives. Human fatherhood did not invent the idea and project it upward onto God; God is Father first, eternally, in his own being, and human fathers are creaturely, partial reflections of it. And “every family in heaven and on earth” reaches wider than human households — every ordered community of creatures, angels included. None is the original; all are derivatives.

Paul says this because he is about to ask the Father for something enormous, and he wants us to know who is being addressed: not a distant deity of unknown character, but the one who most fully embodies everything fatherhood is meant to be — provision, protection, belonging, love, inheritance. Every good father you have known is a dim echo of this one. And for anyone whose earthly father was absent, harsh, or cruel: your experience is not the standard by which God is measured. He is the standard, and the distortions you knew were distortions of an original that is undistorted and unfailing (cf. Luke 15:20–24; Ps. 68:5; Isa. 64:8).

verseByVerse.quote: That according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first request is for power — but not the kind anyone would instinctively ask for. Not power over circumstances, not health or protection from difficulty. Power in the inner being. It is an unusual thing to pray for, and it reveals what Paul thinks the Christian life actually requires. And he asks it “according to the riches of his glory” — not out of God’s riches, as though from an account that could run low, but according to them, the scale of the gift matching the scale of the Giver.

The “inner being” (eso anthrōpon) is the interior self no one else sees — your will, your faith, your capacity to trust God when nothing visible supports it. Picture two people facing the same illness or grief: from outside they look alike, but one is quietly falling apart while the other is genuinely anchored — not unaffected, but held somewhere the storm cannot reach. The difference is not temperament but the condition of the inner person. “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16) — words Paul wrote from the same prison: the outer man in chains, the inner man being renewed, both true at once.

This strengthening is not a vague upgrade; it does specific things. It holds you when faith is hard and prayer feels like talking to the ceiling, keeping the will fixed on God when feeling gives out. It gives endurance when suffering is long — “strengthened with all power… for all endurance and patience with joy” (Col. 1:11). It produces love that costs something, when natural love has run out. And it gives a peace that does not depend on circumstances, guarding the heart in the middle of unresolved trouble (Phil. 4:7).

And notice what Paul prays instead of: not that their circumstances would improve, but that their interior would be strengthened. Because a person with a strong inner life can navigate any circumstance, while a person with a weak one cannot be rescued by even the best external conditions. God’s primary work is not rearranging the furniture of your circumstances but building something in you that cannot be shaken by whatever they bring (cf. Rom. 7:22; Isa. 40:29–31).

verseByVerse.quote: So that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, that you, being rooted and grounded in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things fill this verse. First, “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” The word for dwell is katoikeō — to take up permanent residence, to move in and unpack — as against paroikeō, to lodge temporarily. Paul prays not that Christ would visit in a crisis and then go quiet, but that he would be genuinely at home at the centre of you — in the ordinary Monday, at work, in the argument with your spouse, in the moment of temptation. The Christ who merely visits shows up on Sunday and disappears on Monday; the Christ who dwells is present in both.

“Through faith” is the channel — not a one-time decision but an ongoing posture, the daily turning of the heart to Christ, the habit of asking what he says about this before acting. It is possible to be a real Christian and still push him to the margins, giving him a guest room rather than the master bedroom. Paul prays he would be fully at home — “abide in me, and I in you… apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5).

Then two pictures: “rooted and grounded in love.” The first is from nature. A tree is only as strong as its hidden roots; everything above ground — its height, its fruit, its standing in a storm — depends on what is underground. To be rooted in love is to send your roots down into the certainty of being loved by God, not because you earned it but because that is the kind of God he is. When the storm comes — loss, failure, accusation — the deeply rooted believer bends but does not fall, because they know what the wind cannot change: I am loved; that is not in question. The shallow-rooted, whose sense of God’s love rises and falls with their performance, have nothing to hold them, because the very thing they leaned on is what the storm attacks.

The second picture is from building. A house is only as safe as its unseen foundation; on sand it shifts, on rock it holds (Matt. 7:24–27). To be grounded in love means love — not rules, not performance, not fear — is the bedrock the whole structure rests on. A faith built on moral achievement cracks when you fail badly enough; a faith built on fear either crushes you with guilt or bolts when the pressure lifts. But the one grounded in love, held not by their performance but by the love of the one who laid the foundation, does not shift. Paul doubles the image — roots and foundation, nature and architecture — so the point cannot be missed: love is not the decoration on top of the Christian life; it is the ground beneath it (cf. Rom. 8:38–39; 1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The comprehension Paul prays for is corporate — “with all the saints.” The dimensions of Christ’s love are greater than any one believer or culture can contain; the whole church together is needed even to begin to grasp them. (Which is why theological isolation — reading only one tradition, knowing only one kind of believer — quietly diminishes the soul.)

He names four dimensions — breadth, length, height, depth. Many preachers map these onto the cross (the arms, the upright, and so on); it preaches well, but Paul does not make that link, and he almost certainly means something else. Four directions were the ancient way of describing the totality of all space — up, down, left, right, forward, back, everywhere. Paul is saying the love of Christ fills every direction as far as you can go: no edge, no ceiling, no floor. Go as far as you can in any direction and the love is still there, as deep and wide as when you started.

Feel your way into each. Its breadth: wide enough to include you — your history, your failures, your doubts — and the person beside you whose life looks nothing like yours, and every soul the Father has given the Son across every nation. It has never met a person and thought, this one is too far out. Its length: from before the foundation of the world (1:4) to beyond the last age; it did not begin when you became loveable and it ends never — “neither death nor life… will be able to separate us” (Rom. 8:38–39). Its height: high enough to seat you in the heavenly places (2:6) and bring you before the Father with boldness (3:12), lifting you above your circumstances into the reality of being beloved in God’s sight. Its depth: deep enough to reach you where you actually are — not where you pretend to be — the depths of shame, addiction, grief, the thing you have never told anyone; it goes as deep as sin has gone, for “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

And Paul prays that you would “know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” — not a contradiction. You can know facts about the ocean without ever standing on the shore and feeling its scale. Paul wants you on the beach, feeling the spray, understanding in your bones that the ocean has no other shore — a knowing that changes how you walk through the day because you have been personally, overwhelmingly met by a love you could never have manufactured (cf. John 13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer reaches its summit: “that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” It is the largest thing Paul could ask. It does not mean becoming God, or merging into him, or losing your identity in him — the creature remains the creature. It means being filled with everything God gives of himself — his life, his love, his holiness, his joy, his peace — as much as a finite creature can hold of an infinite God.

Picture a jug held under a waterfall. The waterfall is beyond all comparison larger; yet the jug can be completely full — every inch filled, nothing in it except what pours from the fall. The fullness of God is the waterfall; you are the jug. Paul prays that there would be nothing left in you that is not from God — no corner still given to fear, to self-sufficiency, to the old life. In practice this means a life increasingly marked by what God himself is: loving more deeply because he is love, growing in a holiness and a patience not native to your temperament, carrying a joy that does not evaporate when things are hard. None of it by trying harder — all of it the fruit of being filled.

And “be filled” is passive — plērōthēte, not “fill yourselves.” This is the relief in it: the fullness of God is not the reward for a sufficiently disciplined life; it is a gift. The jug does not fill itself; it holds itself under the water. Your part is not to generate the fullness but to stay open to it — returning to the source through prayer, the word, worship, honest confession, the company of the saints (Paul will make it a command in 5:18, “be filled with the Spirit,” present tense, ongoing).

Paul ends here because nothing beyond this can be asked. The prayer will not be fully answered this side of glory — a finite creature cannot hold the fullness of an infinite God until this life’s limits are removed — but it is answered increasingly as you grow in Christ, and completely when you see him face to face and are made like him (1 John 3:2). That is where the prayer points, and what it will feel like to arrive (cf. Col. 2:9–10; Eph. 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends the prayer not with a quiet amen but with a burst of praise. He has asked enormous things — inner strength, the indwelling Christ, the fullness of God — and now steps back: the God I have been praying to can do immeasurably more than all of it. More than I asked, more than I could imagine asking. The phrase “far more abundantly” is huperekperissou, one of the most extravagant compounds in the Greek New Testament — beyond, out of, overflowing, all stacked together, because no single word goes far enough. This God does not do exactly what is requested and stop; he exceeds the request before the prayer is finished.

And the measure is “the power at work within us” — energoumenēn, presently, actively operating inside you now. Not dormant, not waiting to be switched on by enough faith. Working. And Paul has already named it (1:19–20): the same power that raised Jesus from the dead and seated him at the Father’s right hand. That power is at work in every ordinary believer going about an ordinary day.

Then why does it so often not feel like it — the same old sin, the same weakness? Three things. The power works whether it is felt or not: a seed breaking through concrete is imperceptible day to day, but it is happening — “the inner self is being renewed day by day” even as the outer self wastes away (2 Cor. 4:16). It is aimed first at the inner person, not the outer circumstances: you may be waiting for the power to change your situation while God is using the situation to deploy his power in your character. And it is most visible in weakness — “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9); the one who has run out of their own strength is exactly where they discover that something else takes over — not their power plus God’s, but God’s power where theirs used to be (cf. Phil. 4:13; Rom. 8:11).

verseByVerse.quote: to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great prayer ends where all true prayer must — with God, not with the requests. And you may wonder: what does it actually mean to give God glory? Is it just religious language for being grateful, something that happens in a service and nowhere else? Glory is kābôd/doxa — weight, the overwhelming reality of who God is (as in 1:17). To give him glory is not to add anything to him, as though he grew more glorious by our saying so; the sun does not brighten because someone looks at it. It is to recognise and declare what is already true of him, and to live consistently with it.

That takes three ordinary forms. There is honest praise — when you kneel by your bed on a Tuesday night, no audience, and say, “you are good and I am not; you saved me when I had nothing to offer, and I am grateful.” Gratitude is glory in its simplest form (Ps. 50:23). There is a life that points to him — when you are patient with a difficult colleague and they wonder, what does he have that I don’t?, and the answer turns out to be Christ, God has been glorified without a religious word spoken; “whether you eat or drink… do all to the glory of God” (Matt. 5:16; 1 Cor. 10:31). And there is trusting him when it is hard — “I do not understand this, but I trust you” — perhaps the deepest form, because it says to every watching soul that this God is worth trusting even when it costs: “though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15).

Paul names two places where the glory is displayed: “in the church and in Christ Jesus.” In Christ supremely — the cross and resurrection are its definitive display; and in the church — not a building or a denomination but a people, the community of forgiven sinners where that display goes on. Which means you are not a spectator of something happening elsewhere; you are one of the places where God’s glory is meant to be visible in the world. And “throughout all generations, forever and ever” — your Tuesday-night prayer is no small thing that vanishes by morning; it joins the unbroken chorus rising from every generation of believers, and it will still be echoing when time itself has finished. Amen.

4.title: Unity, Gifts, and the New Self
4.text: <sup>1</sup>I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called, <sup>2</sup>with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, <sup>3</sup>eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. <sup>4</sup>There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — <sup>5</sup>one Lord, one faith, one baptism, <sup>6</sup>one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. <sup>7</sup>But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. <sup>8</sup>Therefore it says, “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.” <sup>9</sup>(In saying, “He ascended,” verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Walk Worthy: The Unity of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Therefore. The great hinge of the letter. Three chapters of indicative — what God has done in Christ, what we have been given, who we are — and now three chapters of imperative: walk worthy. The imperative is entirely grounded in the indicative, and this sequencing is not accidental. Paul never tells us to become something we are not; he tells us to become in practice what we already are in Christ. The Christian life is not the achievement of a new status; it is the outworking in daily experience of a status already secured in the heavenly places. You are already chosen, adopted, redeemed, sealed. Now walk like it.

The first and most foundational imperative is the preservation of unity — and the way Paul frames it is telling. He does not say "create unity" or "achieve unity." He says "maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (v.3). The unity already exists; the Spirit has already made one body. The question is not whether it is real but whether it is visible, whether our daily behaviour reflects the theological truth of our oneness in Christ. And the means of maintaining it are not structural or organisational but dispositional: all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.

The sevenfold "one" that follows (vv.4–6) is the theological bedrock of this unity — and it moves from the experiential to the ultimate. One body, one Spirit, one hope: the dimensions of our shared life. One Lord, one faith, one baptism: the shared confession and initiation. One God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all: the ultimate ground, the Father in whom all the "ones" find their source and their destination. The unity of the church is rooted in the unity of the triune God. We are one because He is one — and because He has made us one in His one Son by His one Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Unity of the Church as Theological Reality

The passage reveals that the unity of the church is not an aspiration or a programme — it is an ontological reality that precedes and grounds every effort to express it. The Spirit has already created one body. The question is not whether unity exists but whether our behaviour honours the unity that does. This distinction between the given reality and the required response is characteristic of Paul's ethical method throughout the letter: indicative first, imperative second. Be what you are. Express what is already true.

The four virtues through which unity is maintained — humility, gentleness, patience, forbearance — are a portrait of Christlike character applied to community life. They are not soft virtues; they are demanding ones. Humility means thinking of others' interests above your own (Philippians 2:3). Gentleness (praus) is the word used of Jesus ("I am gentle and lowly in heart," Matthew 11:29) — strength in service of love. Patience is the willingness to absorb rather than retaliate. Forbearance is the daily choice to keep choosing the person in front of you rather than withdrawing when they disappoint. Together these virtues create the environment in which the given unity of the Spirit can be made visible.

The Reformers consistently emphasised that doctrinal unity and relational unity are inseparable. The sevenfold "one" of vv.4–6 grounds the relational unity of vv.2–3 in doctrinal reality. We are not called to unity by ignoring our differences or pretending that doctrine doesn't matter. We are called to unity because there is genuinely one Lord, one faith, one baptism — and the body that confesses these things is, by that very confession, one. Preserving this unity is not sentimentality; it is theological faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was the most socially diverse community in the city. Former Artemis worshippers, Jewish converts, Greek philosophers, slaves and freedmen, wealthy merchants and harbour workers — all brought together by the preaching of the gospel. The centrifugal forces were enormous. Every human instinct would have been to fracture along existing social fault lines. Paul's "therefore" connects the unity he calls for directly to the cosmic reality of chapter 2: the wall has already come down. The body is already one. Now: walk like it. Bear with one another. Choose the humility that makes room for people unlike you. This was not a small ask in first-century Ephesus.

Now: The church in our age is under intense pressure to fragment — along political lines, cultural lines, worship-style lines, theological nuance lines. The market logic of contemporary Christianity encourages us to shop for churches that suit our preferences, reinforcing the very homogeneity that Paul's vision challenges. Against this, Ephesians 4:1–6 calls the church to a costly unity rooted not in shared preference but in shared confession: one Lord, one faith, one baptism. The local church that perseveres through its internal differences — that chooses patient, humble, forbearing love over the easier path of fragmentation — is doing something more theologically significant than it knows. It is bearing witness to the one God who is over all and through all and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“A prisoner for the Lord” — Paul’s authority to urge is grounded in his suffering for the gospel. He is not a comfortable advisor; he is a man in chains for what he is about to ask of them. The moral weight of the appeal is proportional to the cost the appellant has paid.

“Walk worthy” — axios literally means “of equal weight,” like the two pans of a balance scale. The life should be the equal-weight expression of the calling. The calling has been described in chapters 1–3; everything in chapters 4–6 is the equal-weight life. The gap between the calling and the walk is the space in which sanctification happens.

verseByVerse.quote: With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four qualities that progress. Humility was not a virtue in the Greco-Roman world — it described the servile posture of a slave. Paul redefines it as the foundational Christian character; Jesus modelled it at the washing of feet and on the cross. Gentleness is not weakness but controlled strength — power that has chosen to restrain itself for the sake of another.

Patience is long-suffering toward people, not just circumstances. “Bearing with one another” — the word means to put up with, to hold the weight of another’s difficulty. Love is what makes the others sustainable: without it, humility becomes self-abasement, gentleness becomes passivity, and patience becomes resentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Maintain” — not create or achieve but guard and preserve. The unity already exists (vv. 4–6 will describe it); the calling is to not break it. “The bond of peace” — peace is the ligament that ties the members together; there is no visible unity without peace between persons.

“Eager” means urgent effort, zealous application. Unity is a gift of the Spirit, but maintaining it in a fallen world — among people who disagree, hurt each other, have different preferences, carry different wounds — requires everything we have (cf. John 17:21).

verseByVerse.quote: There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sevenfold confession is Trinitarian in structure: one Spirit (v. 4), one Lord/Christ (v. 5), one God and Father (v. 6). “One body” — the church is not a collection of individuals but a single organism. “One Spirit” — the same Spirit who sealed every believer indwells the whole without division. “One hope” — the final, eternal destiny of all believers is identical; we are all running toward the same finish line. (Eschatological is simply the theological word for “having to do with the last things — the resurrection, the return of Christ, the new creation.” You will meet it often; now you know what it means.) “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” — faith and baptism are not personal achievements but marks of belonging to the one Lord who claimed his people. The unity Paul urges in vv. 1–3 is not created by human effort; it is the visible expression of a unity grounded in the very life of the triune God.

Why does the Trinitarian structure matter? Because it means Christian unity is not merely organisational or emotional — it is theological. We are one because the Father, Son, and Spirit are one, and we are caught up into that life. The church that divides and splinters over secondary matters is acting against its own deepest nature. The three-person God is the pattern; the one body is meant to reflect it. When the church is genuinely united, it is displaying something of the character of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sevenfold confession reaches its summit in the Father. Three prepositions describe three modes of his engagement with his world: over all (sovereignty, transcendence), through all (providential working in and through all things), in all (immanent presence). This is not pantheism but the living God who simultaneously transcends, sustains, and indwells his creation and his redeemed people. When the church fractures into factions, it contradicts the nature of the one God who is Father of all his children — which is why the plea for unity (vv. 1–3) is grounded here in the very character of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having called the church to unity, Paul introduces the glorious diversity that serves it — and its source is the most unexpected one imaginable: the triumphant, ascended, gift-giving Christ. Paul quotes Psalm 68, a victory psalm describing God ascending Mount Zion after defeating his enemies, distributing plunder to his people. He applies it to Christ: the One who descended to the lowest depths of the earth — to death itself, to the far country of human ruin — and then ascended far above all the heavens, has taken the spoils of his victory and distributed them as gifts to his beloved people. And the gifts are not impersonal endowments. They are people. Christ gives gifted persons to his church — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — as the ongoing fruit of his conquest.

But notice first what Paul calls the grace they carry: not saving grace — that has already been lavished in chapters 1–3 — but enabling grace, grace fitted for service, grace for ministry. And its source is Trinitarian: the gifts are given here by Christ the Son (vv. 7, 11); in 1 Corinthians 12 the same gifts flow from the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and the Father (v. 6). One generosity, three Persons. The giftedness of every believer is a testimony to the Trinity.

And the ascended Christ who gives these gifts is himself the one who “fills all things” (v. 10) — plēroō ta panta. This is the great fullness theme that pulses through the whole letter: the church is his fullness (1:23), the goal of every believer is to be filled with all the fullness of God (3:19), the target of every ministry is the fullness of Christ (4:13). The mission of the exalted Lord is to fill all of creation with his presence, his glory, his life. The church is the first instalment of that filling. To serve in this body is to participate in the most significant project in the universe.

The four gifted offices — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — are not interchangeable. The apostles and prophets belong to the foundational era: they laid the once-for-all deposit of Scripture and revelation on which the whole church stands. The evangelists press outward to where the gospel has not yet reached. The pastor-teachers build up what remains, week by week, year by year, through patient feeding of the word. Each equips the saints in their own way: through the apostolic Scriptures, through the whole counsel of God applied to conscience and life, through training every member to be a witness, through the slow, faithful formation of souls.

And the purpose of this equipping subverts every instinct toward a passive, receiver-only congregation. The saints do the ministry; the gifted leaders equip the saints to do it. The congregation is not the audience; it is the army. The pastor is not the performer; he is the trainer. Diakonia — service — belongs to every member: serving the poor, encouraging the struggling, teaching and discipling one another, praying, giving, witnessing. No gift is too small. No calling too ordinary. The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home for a small group, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are building the body of Christ.

The goal is breathtaking: unity of the faith, full knowledge of the Son of God, mature manhood, nothing less than the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Not a few exceptional souls reaching great heights, but the whole body — every member — growing together toward the complete image of Christ. This growth is mature, not merely numerical. It is deep, not merely wide. It means speaking the truth in love — not merely in a pleasant tone, but with the costly, goal-directed love that aims at the health of the other person and the glory of Christ, the love that risks the relationship for the sake of the soul (cf. Prov. 27:6; Gal. 4:16).

The result, when every part is working properly, is a body that builds itself up in love (v. 16): growing more mature, more loving, and more attractive to a watching world. Most of this growth is invisible — the unseen ligament, the quiet conversation, the faithful prayer. But it is real, and it is aimed at the most glorious end imaginable: a church that together reflects the full stature of Jesus Christ, the one who fills all things, until God is all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to His church. The one who has "ascended far above all the heavens" (v.10) is also the one who "fills all things" — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to His wisdom and His grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows "when each part is working properly" — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not "How well am I performing?" but "How well am I equipping?" And the question for every member is not "Am I being fed?" but "Am I contributing?"

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “but” is a pivot from the corporate unity of verses 1–6 to individual gifting. Diversity within unity. Hekastō — to each one, without exception. No member of the body is ungifted. The measure is determined by Christ; he gives as he sovereignly wills. This is not earned, not developed from natural talent alone, but graciously bestowed by the ascended Lord.

Notice carefully what Paul calls it: grace. But this is not saving grace — the grace of justification already lavished on the Ephesians in chapters 1–2. This is enabling grace: grace fitted for service, grace that equips each member to fulfil their particular calling in the body. The same word, but a distinct work. God’s grace does not stop at the threshold of salvation; it floods every room of the Christian life, including the room of ministry.

And mark the Trinitarian richness here. Paul says the gifts are given by Christ (v. 7, cf. v. 11 “he gave”). Yet in 1 Corinthians 12, the same gifts are distributed by the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and their diversity traced to the Father (v. 6). Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — one divine generosity, flowing from three Persons. The giftedness of the church is itself a testimony to the Trinity. cf. 1 Cor. 12:4–6.

Many a believer does not feel gifted. This verse insists otherwise: every believer has received grace for ministry. The question is not “do I have a gift?” but “am I using what Christ has given me?” And whoever uses it is drawing on the inexhaustible generosity of the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 — a psalm of divine-warrior triumph (a song celebrating God as the conquering king returning victoriously from battle, leading his defeated enemies in a triumphal procession, and distributing the plunder to his people) — and applies it to Christ’s ascension. The original psalm celebrated God’s victory over his enemies and triumphal procession to Zion. Paul sees this fulfilled and surpassed in Christ: the risen Lord has ascended “on high,” leading his defeated enemies in his train, and from the position of exaltation he now distributes gifts to his people. The cross was the decisive battle; the ascension is the triumphal procession; the gifts to the church are the spoils of war distributed to the victors. Ferguson: “The church’s gifts are not human resources organized for divine ends; they are the plunder of Christ’s victory given to his people.”

Who are the captives Christ led in his train? Old Joe wants to know. In the original Psalm 68, the captured enemies were the defeated nations and their gods, dragged behind the conquering king in his victory parade — humiliated, stripped of power, displayed as trophies. Paul applies this to what Christ accomplished on the cross and in his resurrection and ascension. The enemies Christ leads captive are the very powers that once held humanity enslaved:

  • Sin — the power that condemned us and kept us from God. Christ bore its full penalty on the cross, so that it no longer has the last word over those who are in him (Rom. 8:1–3).
  • Death — the final enemy, the one no human being had ever defeated. Christ walked into death and came out the other side. Death is not abolished yet — believers still die — but it has been stripped of its sting and its finality (1 Cor. 15:54–57; Heb. 2:14–15).
  • The devil and his spiritual forces — the rulers, authorities, and cosmic powers that Paul will return to in chapter 6. On the cross, Christ disarmed them and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them (Col. 2:15 — the most direct parallel to this verse in Paul’s letters). They are not yet destroyed, but they are defeated: their authority over the believer is broken, their accusations answered, their ultimate doom certain.
  • The law as a condemning power — not the law itself, which is holy and good, but the law’s power to condemn those who have broken it. Christ fulfilled it perfectly and bore its curse in our place (Gal. 3:13), so that it no longer stands against us.

The picture Paul is painting is breathtaking: Christ is not a victim who somehow survived. He is the conquering general, returning in triumph with his defeated enemies on display behind him, ascending to the throne of the universe, and then — from that position of total victory — distributing gifts to his people. The cross looked like defeat. The ascension reveals what it really was: the most decisive victory in the history of the universe. And from the spoils of that victory, he gives the church apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastor-teachers. Every gift in your congregation is loot from the battlefield of Calvary.

The textual adaptation preachers must address: The Hebrew of Psalm 68:18 reads läqa&htilde;tä mattanôt bä‘ädäm — “you received gifts from/among men.” The LXX follows the same sense. But Paul writes “he gave gifts to men.” This reversal is not a mistake; it is a deliberate and theologically informed adaptation. Three explanations converge: (1) The Targum tradition: the Aramaic Targum of Psalm 68:18 already rendered the verse “he gave gifts to the sons of men,” understanding Moses as the subject who received the Torah on Sinai and then distributed it to Israel. Paul, shaped by synagogue use of the psalm at Pentecost, follows this established interpretive tradition. (2) The logic of the conquering king: in the ancient world, when a victor returned in triumph, he received tribute from the defeated and then distributed gifts to his soldiers. “Receiving” and “giving” were two phases of the same event; the one who received the spoils immediately distributed them. Paul applies the distribution phase because that is the point of his argument: the ascended Christ gives to the church. (3) Christological transposition: where the original psalm may have described Moses ascending Sinai and receiving the law, or God ascending Zion and receiving worship, Paul sees the greater fulfillment: the Son ascends to the Father, receives all authority (Philippians 2:9–11; Acts 2:33), and from that position of exaltation pours gifts upon his people. The Spirit given at Pentecost (Acts 2:33: “having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this”) is precisely the dynamic Paul is invoking. The adaptation is typologically and theologically grounded, not textually careless.

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s parenthetical commentary addresses a logical implication: ascent presupposes prior descent. The eternal Son descended — into the humiliation of incarnation, into the full depth of human experience, into death itself. The one who went down is the one who went up. The descent and ascent together span the entire vertical range of existence, so that the ascended Christ might “fill all things” — permeate all of reality with his presence, lordship, and life-giving power. There is no depth of human suffering where Christ has not gone and from which he has not returned in triumph. Sproul: “There is no place in the universe, no depth of human experience, where Christ has not gone — and from which he has not returned victorious.”

‘The lower parts of the earth’ has been read in two main ways, and both are worth knowing. Most modern Reformed scholars take it to mean the earth itself — “the lower parts, namely the earth” — so the descent is the Incarnation: the eternal Son left heaven and came down to earth. This makes the contrast beautifully simple: heaven above, earth below, ascent out of the place he had entered. The other reading, going back to Chrysostom, Origen, and the tradition behind the Apostles’ Creed (“he descended into hell”), takes “lower parts of the earth” to mean below the earth — the realm of the dead — so that the descent includes Christ’s death and his going to the place of the dead before the resurrection (cf. Psalm 63:9; 1 Peter 3:18–20). Either reading makes the same theological point: Christ’s exaltation to the highest place presupposes his willingness to descend to the lowest. The one who now fills all things is the one who first emptied himself of glory to enter our world. This is the inexhaustible wonder of the Incarnation.

What does it actually mean that Christ “fills all things”? In plain terms: the ascended Christ is not sitting passively in heaven, far removed from your daily life. He who went to the lowest depth and rose to the highest height now fills the entire range of reality with his presence, his lordship, his life. There is nowhere in your experience — no grief so dark, no failure so complete, no situation so hopeless — that Christ has not already been, and from which he has not returned victorious. He does not fill things the way water fills a glass — passively. He fills them the way a king fills his kingdom: with authority, presence, and life-giving power.

“That he might fill all things” — hina plērōsē ta panta — is one of the most majestic phrases in this entire letter, and it is not a stray thought. The word plērō (to fill, to bring to fullness) and its cognates course through Ephesians like a great river. In 1:23 the church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all.” In 3:19 Paul prays that believers might “be filled with all the fullness of God.” In 4:13 the goal of every gift is “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” In 5:18 the imperative is “be filled with the Spirit.” This is not coincidence — it is the theological pulse of the letter. Paul is telling us that the mission of the ascended Christ is the progressive filling of all creation with his glory, his presence, his life.

What does it mean that Christ fills all things? It means he is not absent from any corner of his universe. He who descended to the lowest depth and ascended to the highest height now holds all of reality in the span of his sovereign presence. He fills the cosmos as Lord. He fills the church as Head. He fills each believer by his Spirit. This is not pantheism — Christ does not become creation — but it is something astonishing: the exalted God-man, bearing a glorified human nature, exercises a universal lordship and presence that leaves nothing outside his reach. Creation groans for this fullness (Rom. 8:22). The church is being built toward this fullness. History is moving toward the moment when the filling is complete and God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). cf. Col. 1:17–20; Eph. 1:22–23.

For the preacher and the struggling saint alike, this is breathtaking comfort. There is no situation so empty of hope, no life so hollowed out by grief or sin or loss, that the filling Christ cannot enter it. He who filled the far country of death now fills the far country of your suffering. The one who fills all things has not overlooked you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are not spiritual gifts as such — they are gifted persons given to the church. Christ gives people as gifts. Notice: apostles and prophets are listed first (cf. 2:20 — the foundation), then the continuing offices of evangelist and pastor-teacher. The Greek construction suggests “shepherds and teachers” may be a single office — the pastor who teaches.

The Apostles were those personally commissioned by the risen Christ, eyewitnesses of the resurrection, with authority to speak and write his word with binding force. Paul lists himself in this category despite not having walked with Jesus during his ministry (1 Cor. 9:1; 15:8). Their role was foundational and unrepeatable: the New Testament is their legacy. The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20) — a foundation is laid once. There are no apostles today in this primary sense.

The Prophets here are New Testament prophets, not the great writing prophets of the Old Testament. They received and declared direct revelation from the Spirit, filling in the teaching of the church before the canon was complete (cf. Acts 11:27–28; 13:1–2). Alongside the apostles they belong to the foundational era. With the closing of the canon their revelatory function ceased, though the gift of proclamation — forthtelling rather than foretelling — continues in every preacher who opens the word.

The Evangelists were those especially gifted and called to carry the gospel to those who had not yet heard it — travelling proclaimers of Christ, like Philip (Acts 21:8) and Timothy (2 Tim. 4:5). Their work is not confined to the apostolic age. Wherever the gospel frontier advances, Christ gives evangelists. They are frontier workers: breaking ground, planting churches, moving on. The church needs them in every generation.
