The Shepherds and Teachers (literally poimenas kai didaskalous) are almost certainly a single office, as the Greek article groups them together. This is the pastor-teacher: the one who tends the flock by feeding it the word. The shepherd image stresses care, protection, and knowing the sheep by name (cf. John 10:11–14; 1 Peter 5:1–4); the teacher image stresses the means by which that care is exercised — systematic, faithful, nourishing exposition of Scripture. Where the apostle laid the foundation and the evangelist broke new ground, the pastor-teacher builds up what remains — steadily, patiently, week by week, over a lifetime.

Plain summary for Old Joe: So did the apostles and prophets carry on after the Bible was written? No — those were once-for-all, foundational offices. But Christ still gives the church evangelists — people gifted and called to take the gospel to those who have never heard it — and pastor-teachers — the men who preach and shepherd God’s flock Sunday by Sunday, year by year. These two offices are alive and well today. Every faithful pastor, every gospel-carrying missionary, is a gift from the ascended Christ to his church. He did not leave his people without the people they need.

Sproul and MacArthur both note that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet were tied to the completion of the canon; the continuing offices are evangelist and pastor-teacher. The church is still built today by those who preach the word. Every faithful pastor stands in this long line of gifted persons whom Christ himself has given to his church — a humbling and glorious calling, and a reason to honour and pray for the pastors Christ has given you.

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the most transformative verses in ecclesiology. The purpose of the gifted leaders is not to do the ministry for the saints but to equip (the word used for mending nets, setting bones: fitting something for its proper function) the saints so that they do the work of ministry. The building up of the body is the saints’ work, under Word-shaped leadership.

The practical implication is staggering: a healthy church is not one where a gifted minister does everything, but one where the whole body is equipped and active. Pastoral ministry is not performance; it is preparation (cf. Rom. 12:4–5; 1 Cor. 12:7).

How are the saints equipped? Paul does not leave this vague. Each of the four offices of verse 11 equips in its own way, together forming a complete environment of formation:

  • Through the apostles — the saints are equipped by the apostolic writings: the New Testament Scriptures, which carry the full weight of Christ’s own authority. Every time the word is opened and preached, the apostles are still equipping the church. The canon is not a closed archive; it is a living instrument.
  • Through the prophets — the saints are equipped by the whole counsel of God’s word, Old and New Testament, which the prophetic tradition gave us. Proclamation that opens this word — applying it to conscience, rebuking sin, stirring hope — is the prophetic voice still at work in the pulpit.
  • Through the evangelist — the saints are equipped not only by hearing the gospel but by seeing it preached and learning to share it themselves. A healthy evangelist does not merely win converts; he trains the congregation to be witnesses in their own households, workplaces, and neighbourhoods.
  • Through the pastor-teacher — the saints are equipped by systematic, patient, week-by-week feeding of the word: doctrine that shapes the mind, exhortation that moves the will, and pastoral care that tends individual souls. This is the slow work of katartismō — mending, fitting, maturing — applied person by person, year by year.

The result Paul envisions is a congregation of ministers, not a minister with a congregation. Every member fitted for their function. Every joint contributing (v. 16). This is the church in full health.

What kind of ministry can members do? Paul uses the broad word diakonia — service — deliberately. It is not restricted to pulpit or platform. The New Testament fills in the picture richly:

  • Serving and practical care — meeting practical needs: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, caring for widows, welcoming the stranger (Matt. 25:35–36; Rom. 12:13; James 1:27). This is ministry as much as preaching.
  • Encouragement and exhortation — speaking words that strengthen faith, comfort the grieving, and call the wandering back (Heb. 3:13; 1 Thess. 5:11). Every believer can do this.
  • Teaching and discipling — instructing others in the faith, whether formally in a small group or informally one-to-one (Col. 3:16; 2 Tim. 2:2; Titus 2:3–5). Older saints teaching younger. Fathers and mothers teaching children.
  • Evangelism and witness — telling neighbours, colleagues, and family about Christ. Not everyone is an evangelist by office, but every member is a witness by calling (Acts 1:8; 1 Peter 3:15).
  • Prayer — intercession for one another, for the church, for the lost, for rulers (Eph. 6:18; 1 Tim. 2:1). Prayer is not the least of ministries; it may be the most powerful.
  • Giving — the ministry of generous, joyful giving that funds gospel work and sustains those in need (2 Cor. 9:6–8; Phil. 4:17–18). Generosity is a form of building the body.

No gift is too small and no calling too ordinary to be included in diakonia. The woman who quietly visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home for a small group, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are doing the work of ministry. Christ gave the gifted leaders so that this becomes every member’s normal life.

What does “building up the body of Christ” mean? The image is architectural — oikodomē, the construction of a building (cf. 2:21–22 where the church is a temple being built). But the building is alive: it is a body, and it grows. Paul holds both images in tension deliberately, because no single metaphor is large enough for what the church is.

Building up the body means at least three things working together:

  • Numerical growth — new members added as the lost are converted and welcomed in. The body grows by addition. Evangelism is not optional; it is part of the building project (cf. Acts 2:47).
  • Maturity and depth — each existing member growing in knowledge, faith, love, and Christlikeness (vv. 13–15). A church can grow numerically and still be immature — Paul’s concern here is primarily that the body reaches “mature manhood, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (v. 13). This happens through the word, prayer, suffering, and the mutual ministry of members to one another.
  • Unity and cohesion — the joints being fitted, the parts working properly together (v. 16). A body that is growing but fragmented is not healthy. Love is the mortar (v. 16b). Building up the body always has a corporate, relational dimension: you cannot build the body by yourself, alone.

Ultimately, building up the body of Christ is participating in the very purpose of God for history. The church is not a social club that God happens to approve of; it is “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (1:23). To serve one another faithfully in the smallest act of diakonia is to contribute to something of eternal and cosmic significance.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal belongs to the future as well as the present — eschatological simply means “having to do with the final day, the end God is moving all things toward” — and maturity is a direction of travel, not a destination you arrive at in this life. Tēlikia — the full stature, the complete measure of Christ. The contrast in verse 14 is between children tossed at sea and mature adults standing firm. False teaching is the wind; doctrinal depth is the anchor. The solution to theological instability is not suspicion but growth — growing up into Christ through the ministry of the Word.

Paul stacks four phrases here, each one deepening the picture of where all this equipping and ministry is meant to lead. They are not four separate destinations but four angles on a single glorious goal.

“The unity of the faith” — this is not the unity of tolerance, where differences are smoothed over by indifference to truth. It is the unity that comes when the whole body holds the same faith — the apostolic deposit, the gospel received, the confession shared. The article is important: the faith, not merely a personal believing. As the church grows in understanding of what it believes together, division and faction give way to a deep, joyful agreement rooted in the word. This unity is not already fully achieved; it is the direction every sermon, every small group, every act of mutual teaching is aimed at. cf. Jude 3; Phil. 1:27.

“The knowledge of the Son of God” — the Greek is epignōsis, not mere intellectual acquaintance but full, personal, experiential knowing — the kind of knowing that transforms the knower. This is knowledge of a Person, not merely knowledge of a doctrine. The Son of God is not a topic to master but a Lord to know ever more deeply. Calvin wrote that the whole of the Christian life is a progressive knowing of Christ — and that we are never so advanced that we do not need to know him better. The goal of all Christian ministry is not a more informed congregation but a congregation more deeply captivated by Jesus Christ himself.

“Mature manhood” — andra teleion, a complete or perfect man. Paul speaks corporately: the whole church together reaching the maturity of a fully-grown person. Individually, every believer is to leave behind the instability and gullibility of spiritual infancy and reach the settled, rooted, discerning character of an adult. Maturity here is not the absence of struggle but the presence of stability — a faith that is no longer easily capsized. It involves theological depth, moral seriousness, and the relational wisdom to speak truth in love (v. 15). It is what the years of faithful preaching, suffering, prayer, and community are meant to produce.

“The measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” — the most breathtaking phrase of the four. The standard of maturity is not a human benchmark — not the most admirable elder in your congregation, not some abstract ideal of virtue. It is Christ himself in his fullness. Plērōma again — the fullness that fills all things (v. 10), that the church is called to embody (1:23). Paul is saying: the destination is nothing less than the church collectively reflecting the full character, wisdom, love, and glory of Jesus Christ. This will not be fully achieved until the last day — it will not be fully reached until the last day — but it is the real goal, not a figure of speech. Every act of ministry, every word of encouragement, every prayer, every sermon is a small contribution to this staggering end: a people who, together, look like Christ.

“Cunning” in v. 14 translates panourgia — craftiness, the word used of the serpent in Genesis. Doctrinal deception has always employed theological-sounding language. And the antidote is always the same: deep knowledge of the Son of God. The lasting defence is not merely knowing why false teaching is dangerous, but knowing Christ more deeply.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alētheuontes en agapē — truthing in love. Not just speaking truth but living it, embodying it, in a context of love. Truth without love is cold; love without truth is hollow. The maturing church holds both together as it grows into its head.

What truth did Paul have in mind? The context supplies the answer. The preceding verses speak of the apostolic faith (v. 13), the knowledge of the Son of God (v. 13), and the danger of being swept away by false doctrine (v. 14). The truth Paul means is above all the gospel truth — the content of the faith: who Christ is, what he has done, what it means to live in him. It is theological and moral truth together: the truth about God, about humanity, about sin and grace and the new life. It is the truth that the wolves of verse 14 are trying to distort. And it is truth that must be spoken — in preaching, in correction, in personal conversation, in the daily witness of a life aligned with the gospel. Stott writes: “Christians are to be truth-speakers. This has to do with what comes out of our mouths in the company of fellow believers and in the world.” cf. Col. 3:16; 2 Tim. 4:2.

What did “in love” mean? Not primarily “in a nice tone of voice” — though gentleness matters (2 Tim. 2:25). The love Paul has in mind is something deeper and more demanding than pleasantness. It is love with a goal: the good of the other person, the health of the body, the glory of Christ. It means speaking truth for someone rather than at them. It means the motive is not to win an argument, protect a reputation, or score a theological point, but to build up. Love is what separates the surgeon’s scalpel from the bully’s fist — both may cause pain, but only one is aimed at healing. Proverbs 27:6 captures it: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.” And Galatians 4:16, where Paul asks with grief: “Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?” Truth told in love is costly to the speaker. It risks the relationship for the sake of the person.

“Grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ” — the phrase “in every way” is important. Paul does not allow partial growth. It is not enough to grow in knowledge while love withers, or to grow in zeal while wisdom lags. The call is comprehensive: in doctrine, in character, in relationships, in worship, in witness, in suffering — in all of it, the direction is the same: into Christ. He is not merely the model of maturity; he is the substance of it. To grow up is not to become more impressive versions of ourselves; it is to become more like him, more hidden in him, more fully shaped by his mind and heart. The head gives direction to the whole body — Christ’s lordship over every dimension of the church’s life is what Paul is after. Nothing is exempt. No corner of the church’s life, no part of a believer’s character, is permitted to stay immature. cf. Col. 2:19; 2 Cor. 3:18.

Verse 16 is a masterpiece of organic metaphor: Christ is the head from whom the whole body is joined and held together by every supporting ligament, each part working properly, growing the body in love. The church’s health depends on connection to Christ, on the proper working of every member, and on love as the animating principle. MacArthur calls this “the most comprehensive description of church growth in the New Testament.”

“Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love” — what did Paul mean? All three things you might intuit are present, and Paul intends them together:

  • More mature — this is the primary thrust in context. The body grows toward the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Each member, as their part works properly, draws the whole body further from the immaturity of verse 14 and closer to the settled, Christ-shaped wholeness of verse 13. Growth here is deepening: richer doctrine, stronger faith, more Christlike character, more stable love.
  • More loving — love is named as both the means and the end: the body builds itself up in love. This is the same love that grounds unity in verses 1–3, that governs truth-speaking in verse 15, and that will characterise every practical command in verses 25–32. As the body matures it does not simply become more theologically precise; it becomes more warm, more patient, more self-giving. Maturity without growing love is not maturity — it is merely sophistication.
  • Larger in number — Paul almost certainly has numerical growth in view as well. A body that is “working properly” includes the evangelist of verse 11 and the witnessing members of verse 12. A healthy organism grows outward as well as inward. As the body is built up in love, it becomes attractive to the world — Jesus said as much: “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). A church overflowing with the love described here is itself an instrument of evangelism.

What does this look like in practice? Paul’s image of joints and ligaments is deliberately concrete. He is not describing a mystical experience but an organic, structural reality. In practice, the self-building body looks like this:

  • The member with the gift of encouragement seeks out the one who is struggling and speaks life into them — a joint doing its work.
  • The small group that studies the word together, prays honestly, and holds each other accountable — ligaments holding the body together under pressure.
  • The older woman who takes time to disciple a younger one in how to love her husband and raise her children (Titus 2:3–5) — a part working properly.
  • The congregation that disagrees over a secondary matter and chooses to absorb the cost rather than fracture — the bond of peace (v. 3) holding under strain.
  • The deacon who visits the sick, the giver who funds the missionary, the intercessor who rises early to pray for the church — all of them building, all of them contributing to growth.

None of this is spectacular. Most of it is invisible. That is precisely Paul’s point: the body grows not through the heroics of a few outstanding individuals but through the faithful, ordinary, daily contribution of every part. The ligament is never seen. The joint is never applauded. But remove them and the body collapses. Every quiet act of service, every honest conversation, every prayer offered for a fellow member — these are the materials from which Christ is building his church. cf. 1 Cor. 12:21–26; Col. 2:19.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from theology to the street. “No longer walk as the Gentiles walk.” Not a gentle suggestion — an apostolic command, issued in the Lord’s name. And the reason it must be commanded is itself the warning: becoming a Christian does not automatically remake your habits. The old gravity is still there. You must walk differently, deliberately, because the new life does not run on autopilot.

The diagnosis is sober: a mind cut loose from God loses its anchor. Not its intelligence — its direction. It thinks hard but goes nowhere. The understanding darkens. The heart hardens — not in a single dramatic moment but through the quiet accumulation of small refusals, each making the next a little easier, until the conscience is worn smooth and the soul no longer notices what it has lost. Sensuality, insatiable craving, the futile pursuit of things that cannot satisfy — this is where the road ends. Paul is not describing monsters. He is describing the trajectory of every unrenewed human heart, including the one that used to belong to these Ephesians.

But they have learned Christ. And that changes everything. The old self — the whole person oriented away from God, rotting through deceitful desires — is to be stripped off like a stinking garment. The mind is to be renewed, daily and continuously, by the Spirit working at the deepest level. The new self — a new creation, bearing the restored image of God in genuine righteousness and holiness — is to be put on. This is not self-improvement. It is resurrection applied to daily life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The "old self" and "new self" of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is "corrupt through deceitful desires" (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be "in Christ" is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: "be transformed by the renewal of your mind." The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is "the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in His image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I say and testify in the Lord” — and that second word is heavier than it looks. The Greek is martyromai, from martys, “witness” — the same root that later gives us martyr, one who testifies to the truth even at the cost of his life. In both everyday and biblical Greek the word belongs to the solemn, legal register: not casual speech but formally calling something to witness, affirming it as true as though under oath. It carries the weight of “I solemnly declare” or “I call you to witness.”

Paul reaches for this same word at his weightiest, most personal moments — when he stakes his own integrity on what he is about to say. He uses it in Galatians 5:3, and, strikingly, in his farewell to the elders of this very church: “I testify to you this day” (Acts 20:26). It is the language of a man putting himself on the line.

So by pairing “say” with “testify,” Paul marks this verse as a turning point. He is not offering friendly ethical advice; he is solemnly attesting, as though standing as a witness before God, that the Ephesians must abandon their old Gentile way of life. And “in the Lord” names the sphere in which he swears it: not on his own private authority, but as a man united to Christ, speaking under his Lord’s own gaze. In short, this is courtroom-weight language: Paul is not suggesting — he is swearing to what he says, staking his own witness on it. This is not advice; it is a sworn charge.

And it is a necessary one. That it has to be issued at all tells us something: conversion does not automatically make us live as God wills. The old patterns do not vanish overnight; the new life must be deliberately walked in. Were it automatic, the command would be pointless.

“No longer walk as the Gentiles do” — these believers had once lived exactly that way. It no longer fits who they have become.

Why single out the Gentiles? Not because unbelieving Jews had it together, but because Paul writes to a mostly Gentile congregation and points to the world they came out of — pagan culture with its many gods, its moral confusion, its chase after pleasure and status with no reference to the living God. That world no longer defines them. Peter says exactly the same thing to his readers: the past was time enough to have lived that way — let it be finished (cf. 1 Pet. 4:3).

“In the futility of their minds” — two words, and both carry weight. “Futility” (mataiotēs) means emptiness: something that promises much but holds nothing when you reach for it. It is the Old Testament word for idols — “vain things,” empty things that cannot see, save, or satisfy (cf. Jer. 2:5). And “mind” (nous) is not narrow brain-power but the whole faculty by which a person weighs what is real and decides how to live. Put the two together and Paul’s diagnosis is exact: not merely muddled thinking, but a mind whose every judgment is bent because the thing at its centre is empty. He writes to Ephesus, a city built around the great temple of Artemis. Picture their old life: praying to a goddess of stone, buying charms and amulets, paying astrologers to read their fate (Acts 19:19), chasing the next festival, pleasure, and rung of status. Busy — religious, even — but aimed at gods who were not there. And there is the madness of it: a man can pour out his whole life — his worship, his labour, his deepest longing — upon something that, in truth, is nothing at all. A mind set on nothing can only produce more nothing — which is exactly the downward chain Paul traces next in vv. 18–19.

Underneath it all is a hunger. God made the human heart for himself, and Augustine said it best: “you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Every person feels that ache and tries to fill it — often with good things: family, work, a hard-earned holiday. These are gifts of God. But good as they are, they were never built to carry the weight of that hunger; they cannot fill a space shaped for God himself. A mind cut off from him is not stupid — often clever and hard-working — but it is reaching for substance in things that have none, and the moral unravelling of vv. 18–19 follows. cf. Rom. 1:21.

This is the whole burden of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher tried everything “under the sun” — pleasure, work, wealth, great building projects, even wisdom itself — and pronounced it all “vanity” (Hebrew hevel: a vapour, a breath you cannot hold). And here is the striking thing: when the Old Testament was put into Greek, that famous refrain — “vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:2) — was rendered with this very word, mataiotēs, the same word Paul reaches for here. Ecclesiastes is the long proof of what Paul says in a phrase: good things, chased without God, come up empty — and the book’s own answer is the cure, “fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12:13).

It is no different today — only the idols have changed their clothes. The man who works flat out for the bigger house, the better car, the title on the door gets all of it, and meets the same hollowness on the other side. The endless scroll; the next purchase; the next achievement that was finally going to satisfy — and never does. Plenty of motion; no destination. That is the futility of the mind — and it is exactly what Christ came to rescue us out of, by giving the restless heart back the only One who can fill it: himself.

And none of this stops at conversion. Old Joe is redeemed — and Old Joe still catches himself reaching for the old empty wells, quietly believing that the next thing will finally fill him. So how does he actually fight it? Not mainly by gritting his teeth and trying to want less; a hungry heart is not talked out of eating. The old Scottish preacher Thomas Chalmers named the real answer — “the expulsive power of a new affection”: you do not drive out a lesser love by willpower, but by a greater one. The cure for misplaced satisfaction is not less desire; it is a bigger desire, fixed on Christ.

In practice that is a few ordinary, repeatable things. When the itch comes — ‘if I just had that, I’d be content’ — Old Joe learns to name it: that is the hunger again, and that thing cannot fill it. He preaches the truth back to himself before the craving talks him into it — this is the daily “renewal of the mind” that turns a person from the inside out (cf. Rom. 12:2). He keeps feeding the real hunger at its only true source — in the Word, in prayer, at the Lord’s table, among God’s people — because a God-shaped space is filled only by God. And he receives the good gifts — his wife, his work, his Saturday rest — not as gods that must satisfy, but as gifts from a Father who already has, which frees him to enjoy them without crushing them under a weight they were never built to carry. That, in the end, is what it means to walk no longer as the Gentiles do.

One last thing — and it changes how this whole verse feels. A Christian can read “you must no longer walk” and hear nothing but duty: I have been given so much; now I had better shape up and do my obligations. But that misses the very heart of it. God is not calling Old Joe out of a good life into a grey one of grim chores. He is calling him out of the empty life into the full one. The walk Paul commands is not the price of being saved; it is the beauty of being saved — the life the human heart was actually made for, the one life that truly satisfies and truly sets a man free. The old way looked like freedom and proved to be a cage; this way looks like surrender and proves to be the open field. To “no longer walk as the Gentiles do” is not to lose your life. It is, at last, to begin really living it.

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul traces a chain of cause and effect — and the direction matters. He names four things, and the little words that join them (“because of the ignorance… due to the hardness”) show he is listing them from the surface down to the root: the darkened understanding is the visible symptom; beneath it lies alienation from the life of God; beneath that, a wilful ignorance; and at the very bottom, the root of it all — a hardened heart. The engine runs the other way from the words: the heart hardens first, and everything else follows downstream. This is not random moral failure; it is the predictable anatomy of a life moving away from God. They are not dark for lack of light — they are dark because, one closed eye at a time, they cut themselves off from the source of life, until the closing became permanent. We will follow Paul’s order — symptom down to root — but keep the true direction in view.

Darkened in their understanding — and mark the form of the word: Paul does not say they darkened themselves, but that they have been darkened. Something was done to them, and the effect abides. Behind every eye a man closes against the light there stands a judgment he did not administer. It is not intellectual stupidity; these people may be brilliant, educated, successful. Paul means the faculty by which a person judges what matters — the inner compass that decides what is worth living for, and therefore where the time, the money, and the energy actually go. When that compass is darkened, the needle still swings confidently; it simply points the wrong way. So this is wider than the occasional moral decision — ‘should I lie here, should I cheat there?’ It reaches the whole shape of a life: what you get up for, what you sacrifice for, what you quietly believe will make you somebody. A thousand individually ‘sensible’ choices, all aimed at the wrong horizon. Paul says the same in Rom. 1:21: they “became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened.” cf. Rom. 1:21.

Back then in Ephesus it looked entirely respectable. A man poured his years into honour and status, into the favour of Artemis and the household gods, into building a name and securing his place in the city — and every neighbour would have nodded that he was living wisely. The choices were not obviously ‘immoral’; they were the normal, admired investment of a life. And they were aimed at gods who were not there and a glory that would not last. The compass felt true. It was broken.

For Old Joe it looks just as respectable. Darkened understanding today is rarely a man choosing evil with his eyes open; it is a decent, hard-working man pouring his one life into things that cannot finally hold it — the career, the retirement number, the renovated house, the children’s success, the quiet evenings handed over to a screen. None of it scandalous. All of it reasonable. And yet, weighed on the scales that matter, much of it is energy spent on a horizon that ends at the grave. That is what darkened understanding does: not mostly make a man wicked, but make the wrong things look like the obvious things to live for — while Christ, the one investment that lasts, quietly seems optional. cf. 2 Cor. 4:4.

But be careful here, Old Joe — do not draw the wrong conclusion. Paul is not saying that work and family are ‘worldly stuff’ that does not matter, as though only going to church and sharing the gospel really counted with God. Many sincere Christians have quietly believed that — and it is not in the Bible. God invented work before sin ever entered the world; he put Adam in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Gen. 2:15). God invented marriage and family and called them good (Gen. 1:28; 2:18). Your job and your home are not a lower, second-class life that the spiritual part has to rise above. For most of us, most of the time, they are the very place the spiritual life is lived.

So the cure was never to do less — to walk away from the desk or neglect the family in order to be ‘more spiritual.’ The compass was the problem, not the road. Take the very same Monday — the same job, the same school run, the same bills — and change the aim. Do the work heartily, “as for the Lord and not for men” (Col. 3:23). Love your wife and raise your children as a trust God has placed in your hands, not as a monument you are building to yourself. Eat, drink, clock in, clock out, “all to the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31). To the neighbour over the fence, nothing need look different. Underneath, everything is: the same hands at the same tasks, no longer trying to fill the God-shaped space, but offered back to the God who already fills it. That is the redeemed mind on an ordinary Monday — not escaping the world, but doing the world’s honest work for a new Master, with a clear horizon at last.

Alienated from the life of God — this is the phrase Old Joe may stumble over, so let us say it plainly. There are two kinds of life. There is the life you can measure — a heartbeat, breath in the lungs, blood in the veins. Every person has that. But there is a deeper life: God’s own life flowing into a soul — knowing him, being at peace with him, the inner man awake and joined to the One who made it. That second life is what Paul means by “the life of God,” and to be alienated from it is to be shut out of it — a stranger to the very thing you were made for.

Picture a flower cut for the table. On Monday it looks perfect — bright, upright, lovely. But it has been cut from its root, and the truth is it is already dying; it simply has not shown yet. That is a person alienated from the life of God: up and about, working, laughing, looking entirely alive — while cut off from the Root they were made to draw their real life from. Jesus said it himself: “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine… apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). The lights are on, but at the centre something has gone quiet. And here is the wonder of the gospel: this is the very thing Christ came to reverse. “You were dead… but God… made us alive together with Christ” (Eph. 2:1, 4–5). He grafts the cut branch back into the Vine; he joins the dead back to Life.

Due to the ignorance that is in them — this is not ignorance for lack of information. It is the ignorance that results from not wanting to know — the darkness of a man who keeps shutting his eyes against the sun and then complains that it is night. Romans 1:21 says they “knew God” but refused to honour him. The darkening produced a wilful not-knowing — the mind that has turned away from God gradually loses the capacity to find its way back. Peter calls the old life a life of “former ignorance” that the called must now leave behind (cf. 1 Pet. 1:14–15).

Due to the hardness of heart — here is the root of it all. Pōrōsis in Greek — a medical term for the calcification of bone, hard tissue forming where there should be living flexibility. The heart that repeatedly resists God eventually stops feeling the resistance. It is not a single dramatic act of rebellion; it is the accumulation of small refusals, each one making the next a little easier.

Pharaoh is Scripture’s great case study, and the two halves of his story must be held together. Again and again we read that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Ex. 8:15, 32; 9:34). And again and again we read that the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Ex. 9:12; 10:1). Both are true, and the order is sobering: the man hardened himself, until God confirmed him in the hardness he had chosen. There comes a point where God gives a man over to the very thing he insisted on having. That is the most frightening sentence a soul can receive — not lightning from heaven, but a handing-over. The judgment is that God stops interrupting. Which is why Scripture pleads, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” — before the heart is “hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (cf. Heb. 3:7–13).

Having become callous — the conscience has been worn smooth. What once produced shame no longer does. What once felt wrong now feels normal. This is the terrifying end of the hardening process: not defiance, but numbness. The person no longer even notices what they have lost.

Have given themselves up to sensuality — Paul’s language here echoes Romans 1: God “gave them up.” But notice — here it is they who give themselves up. Both are true: God releases people into the trajectory they have chosen, and they have actively chosen it. Sensuality (aselgeia) is not merely physical desire — it is shamelessness, appetite with the brakes removed, the pursuit of sensation with no regard for God, conscience, or consequence. Romans makes the same dreadful pairing explicit: because they “did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done” (cf. Rom. 1:28).

Greedy to practise every kind of impurity — the end of the road. The appetite is never satisfied; it always wants more. Impurity covers the whole inner life — not just outward acts but corrupt desires, a mind feeding on what degrades. Sexual sin stands in the foreground here, but the word is wider than the bedroom: it names moral uncleanness of every kind — the greed that treats a person as a thing to be used, the exploitation that builds a fortune on another man’s back, the idolatry practised in the shadow of Artemis’s temple, where worship and vice were sold at the same counter. A man may keep his marriage bed undefiled and still be filthy in Paul’s sense. And “greedy” (pleonexia) tells us that indulgence does not satisfy — it inflames. The person who thought freedom lay in removing all limits discovers they are enslaved to cravings that cannot be fed.

For Old Joe — this chain is a warning, not just a description. None of this begins with a dramatic fall. It begins quietly: a little hardness, a little less sensitivity, a little more drift. The Christian reads this with recognition, not superiority — this was the trajectory we were on. Grace interrupted it. Do not drift back. cf. Rom. 1:21–24.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ!
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But that is not the way you learned Christ.” After the bleak description of vv. 18–19, Paul turns on a dime. That world — darkened, alienated, callous, insatiable — is not what you signed up for. You learned something completely different.

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say “you learned about Christ” or “you learned Christ’s teaching.” He says you learned Christ — a Person, not a curriculum. In the ancient world you learned a philosopher’s ideas; the philosopher himself was just the delivery mechanism. Paul is saying something far more radical: the content of Christian learning is Christ himself. You were not handed a new moral code. You were introduced to a living Person — and knowing him is what changes everything.

This is the sharpest possible contrast with the futile mind of v. 17. The pagan mind drifts because it has no fixed point. The Christian mind has one: a Person who does not change, who is not a theory, who can be known and who makes himself known. That is what you learned. Live like it.

verseByVerse.quote: assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul adds a gentle assumption: “assuming that you have heard him and were taught in him.” He is not doubting their conversion — he is reminding them of what they received. They heard Christ. They were taught in him. To hear Christ in this saving way is the mark of his own: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (cf. John 10:27). This is the basis for everything that follows in vv. 22–24.

Notice the little word: taught in him — not taught by him. Had Paul meant simple agency, that Christ was merely the one who delivered the lesson, he had a ready way to say so — “through him.” He does not reach for it. He writes “in him” — the same incorporative “in Christ” language that saturates this letter: in him, in the Beloved, in Christ Jesus, thirty times and more. It is the language of union, not of mere instruction. The teaching did not arrive from the outside as an information transfer, a parcel of facts handed to you at arm’s length. It happened within the reality of your union with Christ. You do not simply receive facts about him; you are in him when the teaching lands.

This is why the futile, darkened mind of vv. 17–19 could never arrive here — it operates outside that union. And this is why what follows is not a new rulebook posted from a distance. The “put off” and “put on” of vv. 22–24, the practical holiness of vv. 25–32, all of it is instruction from within the sphere of Christ. That is precisely why it can produce a “new self, created after the likeness of God” (Eph. 4:24) rather than one more round of futile moral effort. Real transformation happens only in union with him, never from information handed to us at arm’s length.

“As the truth is in Jesus” — and notice Paul’s exact words. He does not say the truth is Jesus, as though setting an equals sign between them. He says the truth is in Jesus. That little word in is not an equation but a location: the truth is found, lodged, embodied — given a face — in him. And Paul uses the human name deliberately. Not “Christ” the title, but “Jesus” — the man who walked in Galilee, who touched lepers, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, who rose on the third day. Truth is not an abstract system floating free from a person; it has taken flesh in a specific human life. Hold that phrase, for it sets the axis of everything that follows. The truth is in Jesus (v. 21); the old self is corrupted through deceitful desires (v. 22). Truth against deceit — that is the real contest of this passage. The old life is not merely naughty; it is a lie whispered to a man about where his happiness lies. And so what Paul issues here is not a summons out of a beautiful life into a grey one. It is a summons out of a horrible life — darkened, alienated, insatiable, lied to — into the most beautiful life a human being can be given.

When you want to know what truth looks like in flesh and blood — how to treat people, how to forgive, how to suffer — you do not consult a definition. You look at Jesus.

Think of how this works with any great virtue. You could hand a man the dictionary definition of courage — accurate, precise, and utterly bloodless. Or you could point him to the soldier who threw himself on the grenade to save his friends. The definition is true; the soldier is courage with a face — courage you can see and name and follow. Or think of a piano teacher. She can give you the theory of a sonata on paper, every note correct, or she can sit down and play it: “there — that is what it is meant to sound like.” The truth of the music is in the playing. So it is here. In Jesus the truth about God, about righteousness, about what a human life was made to be, stopped being a concept on a page and became a life you can watch. He is the sonata played. The truth you have received is as concrete and as solid as that life — the same “word of truth” Paul has already named, the gospel they heard and believed (cf. Eph. 1:13; John 1:14).

The world around you will say truth is whatever feels right to you — a thing you shape to fit the age. Paul says it is not ours to shape at all. It is fixed, because it is found in a Person — and that Person cannot be revised or customised to suit the times. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Heb. 13:8)

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put off” — where did Paul get this image? The clothing metaphor was not Paul’s invention. It was already common in the ancient world — Greek writers used it for adopting or abandoning a way of life, and Jewish teachers spoke of “clothing oneself” in virtue or vice. What Paul does is give it a sharper, more definitive edge: this is not adjusting your wardrobe but stripping off an entire identity. By “identity” here we mean not merely your job or reputation, but the whole of who you take yourself to be — your deepest loves, loyalties, and habits, the self you live out of and present to the world. Paul says the whole of that old self comes off, like a garment. The image of removing a garment captures something important — it is a deliberate act, it involves the whole person, and the old thing is left behind, not kept for later.

“Your old self” — is this the same as the “old man”? Yes — the ESV “old self” translates a phrase that literally means “old man.” Other translations keep “old man” (KJV, NASB). Paul uses the same phrase in Romans 6:6 (“our old man was crucified with him”) and Colossians 3:9. He does not mean the physical body or the personality. He means the whole human self as it was before Christ — the person you were in Adam, oriented away from God, living for self. It is not a part of you; it is the old you.

Why does Paul say the old self “belongs to” the former manner of life? You might expect it the other way round — surely the former manner of life flowed from the old self? Paul’s phrasing is deliberate. He is saying the old self and the old life are so bound together that you cannot separate them. The old way of living is the old self’s natural habitat; it belongs there, it fits there. Which means: if you want to leave the old life behind, the old self must go with it. You cannot keep the old self and expect new behaviour. The root and the fruit come as a package.

“Corrupt” — does this mean dishonest? No — not in the moral sense of being untrustworthy. Paul means rotting. The underlying word is the word for decay, the deterioration of something that is dying. The old self is not merely flawed; it is in a process of active decomposition, moving toward death. It has no future. This is why Paul says “put it off” — you do not renovate something that is rotting. You remove it.

“Through deceitful desires” — how do desires cause corruption? The desires are called “deceitful” because they make promises they cannot keep. They say: this will satisfy you, this will make you happy, this will fill the gap. They never do. And with each unfulfilled promise, the person goes deeper into the pursuit — and the pursuit is itself the corruption. The more the old self chases what it craves, the more it decays, because it is feeding on things that cannot nourish. It is the picture of a person slowly consuming themselves — not realising that every desire indulged without God is accelerating the rot, not healing it. James names the lure exactly: each person “is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire” (cf. James 1:14). And the believer’s answer is decisive — those who belong to Christ “have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (cf. Gal. 5:24).

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between “put off” (v. 22) and “put on” (v. 24) stands this middle command: be renewed. It is the hinge on which the whole movement turns.

Three things about this command matter.

First, it is continuous — not a one-off experience but a daily process. You do not get renewed once and carry that forward. It is something that must keep happening.

Second, it is something done to you: “be renewed” — not “renew yourself.” The Christian is the recipient here, not the agent. God is doing the renewing; you are receiving it. This rules out both passivity (“do nothing and wait”) and willpower (“try harder”). The Spirit renews; the Christian places themselves in the path of his working. Paul states the paradox elsewhere without a trace of embarrassment: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you” (Phil. 2:12–13). God’s working is not the reason to do nothing; it is the only reason that doing anything is worth the effort. Salvation is not of works — but it is unto them (cf. Eph. 2:8–10).

Third, the place it happens: “in the spirit of your minds.” Not the emotions, not the behaviour — the deepest part of the inner person, the mind’s governing centre. This is why behaviour cannot simply be commanded from the outside. Lasting change goes deeper than conduct; it requires the mind itself to be transformed. Paul said the same thing in Romans 12:2: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”

For Old Joe — what does this mean practically? You cannot manufacture this renewal, but you can pursue the means through which God gives it: Scripture that retrains the mind, prayer that opens the soul to God, honest community, and the regular receiving of the preached word. A Christian who neglects these is not being passive — they are starving the very faculty God is trying to renew.

But take heart — this is a promise before it is a command. The renewing is God’s work, and “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Phil. 1:6). The change is often slow, and some days you will see no progress at all; yet Paul insists it is sure — the Spirit is transforming you “from one degree of glory to another” (2 Cor. 3:18). Think of John Newton, once the hard-hearted captain of a slave ship, a man whose mind was given over to cruelty and greed. God did not renew him in a day. But degree by degree, over a lifetime spent in the path of grace, that same mind was so transformed that he gave the church “Amazing Grace.” Near the end of his life, his memory nearly gone, he could still say: “My memory is nearly gone, but I remember two things: that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour.” That is a renewed mind. And the God who did it for Newton is doing it for you. So do not measure the work by a single day. Keep placing yourself in the path of his grace, and trust him to finish what he has begun. cf. Rom. 12:2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Col. 3:10; Phil. 1:6.

verseByVerse.quote: and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put on the new self” — where did Paul get this image? The same clothing metaphor as v. 22, and already familiar: Greek writers spoke of “putting on” virtues or roles, and Paul uses it elsewhere — “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14), “put on the full armour of God” (Eph. 6:11). Clothing implies a deliberate act: you do not accidentally get dressed. The new self does not happen to you automatically; it is something you reach for and wear.

“Created after the likeness of God” — Paul reaches back to Genesis 1:26, “let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” This is what humanity was made for: to reflect God’s character — to think, love, and relate with his justice and compassion. The fall defaced that image; in Christ it is being restored. The new self is not an improved old self but a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17), shaped back into what humanity was always meant to be.

Yet it is more than Eden restored. Adam was innocent, but he was not safe — untested, and able to fall. The pattern of the new self is therefore not the first Adam but the last (1 Cor. 15:45): Christ, tried in every respect, obedient unto death, risen and glorified — proven, and beyond all falling. That is the destination of the image now being renewed in you. Not a journey back to the garden, but arrival somewhere greater than the garden ever was: a Christlikeness that can never again be lost (cf. Rom. 8:29; 1 John 3:2).

“In true righteousness and holiness” — two dimensions of that image in practice. Righteousness: giving each his due — honesty, justice, love (the word leans toward what we owe our neighbour). Holiness: a life set apart for God, marked by reverence and purity (this word leans Godward, toward consecration). The accent differs, but neither term stays on one side — righteousness is owed to God too, and holiness shows in how we live (cf. “holily and righteously,” 1 Thess. 2:10). And true — not religious performance or outward conformity, but the genuine article: inward reality, not a mask.

How does the Christian actually do this? Paul does not elaborate, and the silence is a clue: it is not complicated. To put on the new self is simply to act from who you now are in Christ, not who you used to be. Picture a child taken off the street and adopted into a noble house. His birth has not changed — but his belonging has, entirely. The old instincts linger: he hoards food, flinches at kindness, waits to be thrown out. Learning to ‘put on’ his new self is nothing more than learning to live as what he now truly is — a son at his father’s table, bearing the family name. He does not earn the sonship by behaving like a son; he behaves like a son because he already is one. So with us (Eph. 1:5): in any moment — a conversation, a decision, a temptation — ask what the person you are in Christ would do, and do it, by faith, before the feeling follows. Paul gives the concrete shape in the very next verses (vv. 25–32): stop lying, tell the truth; stop stealing, work and give; stop bitter words, speak what builds up. One deliberate choice at a time, every morning, until it becomes the new grain of the soul.

And measure this by trajectory, not by perfection. The adopted son still flinches; he is a son all the same. The question God puts to a struggling believer is not whether he has arrived, but which way he is facing — and whether, having fallen, he rises and walks on in the clothes his Father gave him. cf. Rom. 13:14; Col. 3:10–12.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Now Paul lands the rubber on the road. Theology becomes Tuesday morning. Five commands, each grounded in the gospel, each aimed at the one thing that makes the body of Christ function or fail: the daily choices of ordinary people in ordinary relationships.

Tell the truth — because we are members of one another and a body cannot survive on false signals. Deal with anger before the sun goes down — because unresolved grievance is a beachhead the devil will occupy and you will not evict him easily once he is inside. Work and give — because the hands that once took are now instruments of grace. Speak only what builds — because your words can carry grace or corruption to the soul of the person who hears them. Forgive — as God in Christ forgave you. That last phrase is everything. The standard is not proportional. It is not “forgive reasonably.” It is: forgive the way the cross forgave you — absorbing the cost, releasing the debt, not because the other person has earned it but because you have been forgiven the unearnable.

Behind it all stands the Holy Spirit (v. 30) — not an impersonal force but a Person who can be grieved. He grieves at falsehood because he is the Spirit of truth. He grieves at unresolved bitterness because he is the bond of peace. He grieves at corrupting words because he is building a holy body. And the wonder: he grieves — and stays. This is the love that will not let go.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. This word (lupeō) in Greek means to cause sorrow, to wound. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; He is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community He inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase "by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve Him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say "by whom you were sealed unless you grieve Him." The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — "forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was, as we have noted, extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — "speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another" — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: "Do not let the sun go down on your anger" is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls. This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Having put away falsehood” — done already, or something still to do? The form Paul uses describes something that has already happened — or that is assumed to have happened — as the basis for the command that follows. Paul is saying: you have put away falsehood in principle, at conversion, when you put off the old self (v. 22). Now live consistently with that. It is the same logic as Romans 6: you have died to sin — so stop acting as though you haven’t. The putting away is real; the speaking of truth must now match it.

What did Paul mean by “falsehood”? More than outright lying. The word covers the full range of untruth: deliberate lies, yes, but also half-truths designed to mislead, flattery that says what people want to hear rather than what is true, silence when something honest needs to be said, and the careful management of how others see you. Falsehood is any communication intended to create a false impression. Paul has already shown in vv. 17–19 that it belongs to the old life — the life unmoored from God, built on unreality. To keep lying after putting on the new self is to reach back for the old rags.

“Speak truth with his neighbour” — just “don’t lie”? And does “neighbour” mean everyone or just fellow believers? Paul is quoting Zechariah 8:16, so “neighbour” carries the sense of anyone you deal with — truth-telling is not just an internal church standard. But Paul immediately narrows the focus: “for we are members of one another.” That phrase refers to the body of Christ. His primary concern here is truth within the church community, because lying to a fellow member is self-destructive — like one part of a body sending false signals to another. The body cannot function without honest communication between its parts.

And “speak truth” means more than simply not lying. It means being the kind of person whose word can be trusted completely — who says the honest thing even when silence would be easier, who keeps their word in small things and large, who is the same in private as in public. Truth is the oxygen the body of Christ runs on. cf. Zech. 8:16; Rom. 12:5.

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be angry” — is Paul actually commanding anger? The form is a command — the same as “speak truth” in v. 25. But most scholars understand it as permission rather than obligation: not “you must be angry” but “if you are angry — when you are angry — that is permitted.” Paul is quoting Psalm 4:4, and his point is that anger itself is not sinful. There are things you should be angry about. Jesus was angry — at the money-changers in the temple (John 2:15–16), at the hardness of heart that preferred a rule over a man’s healing (Mark 3:5). God himself is described as angry at sin throughout Scripture. Anger at injustice, cruelty, or wickedness is a right and appropriate response. To never be angry at anything is not holiness — it is indifference.

“And do not sin” — so anger itself is not the sin? Correct. The sin is not the anger; the sin is what you do with it. Here is a brief example. Your colleague at work takes credit for something you did. You feel angry — and that anger is legitimate, it is a response to an injustice. That anger is not sin. But if you then go and tell everyone else in the office what he did, or if you start deliberately undermining him, or if you lie awake that night rehearsing it and adding to it — now the anger has crossed into sin. The anger was right; what it became was not.

“Do not let the sun go down on your anger” — what should you actually do? Deal with it before the day ends. Paul is not saying you must have every conflict fully resolved by sunset — that is not always possible. He is saying: do not go to sleep still nursing it. Before the day closes, do something: go to the person if you can, or at minimum release the anger to God in prayer — hand it over rather than carrying it into the next day. The danger is not the anger itself but what happens to it overnight. Anger nursed through the night has a way of hardening. What was a legitimate grievance in the evening becomes resentment by morning, and resentment by next week has turned into something darker still. Deal with it while it is still fresh and still manageable. cf. Matt. 5:23–24; Matt. 18:15.

verseByVerse.quote: and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And” — does Paul mean “in addition” or “as a result”? Almost certainly option 2. The little word “and” can simply add another thought, but in context Paul is showing the consequence of ignoring the warning about the sun going down. The flow is: do not let anger remain overnight — because if you do, you are giving the devil a foothold. The “and” links the two halves as cause and effect, not as two unrelated instructions. Verse 27 is the reason behind verse 26.

What did Paul mean by “giving opportunity to the devil”? The word topos means a place, a position — the image is of a military beachhead, a foothold inside your lines from which an enemy can now operate. Paul is not being dramatic. He is being precise: unresolved anger creates a specific opening that the devil actively exploits.

A brief example. Two elders in a church disagree sharply over a decision. Words are exchanged. Neither man goes to the other to clear the air — it feels awkward, and after all, the matter was technically settled. A week passes. They are polite on Sunday but something has cooled. Three months later, the congregation can feel a subtle tension in the leadership without quite naming it. People begin to sense which elder they are more comfortable around. Within a year there are two quiet camps. No one planned this. No dramatic falling-out happened. But a small, unresolved anger was given time to harden — and the devil, who is in no hurry, used it. That is the foothold: not a dramatic assault, but a slow occupation that began with one evening when neither man dealt with the thing before the sun went down.

For Old Joe: the enemy does not need to tempt you into great sin if he can get you to leave a small wound unattended. That is all a foothold requires. cf. 2 Cor. 2:10–11: “so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.”

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Were there really thieves in the church? Evidently — Paul does not write hypothetically. Remember who filled these congregations: day-labourers, dock-workers, household slaves, people living hand to mouth in a world with no safety net. Petty theft was woven into survival — pilfering from a master’s stores, skimming from goods handled at the harbour, ‘forgetting’ to return what was borrowed. Much of it was so common that the culture barely blinked. Paul does: in the body of Christ, the common thing is no longer the acceptable thing.

Watch the shape of the command — three steps, and the third is the surprise. Stop stealing; work honestly instead; so that you may have something to give. Paul does not stop at “stop.” The gospel never merely empties a life; it refills it, aimed the other way. The stated purpose of honest work is not respectability, not even self-sufficiency, but generosity — the hand that once took becomes the hand that gives. Begg notes this is one of the most quietly radical ethical statements in the New Testament: the cure for taking is not just keeping your hands to yourself — it is opening them. Zacchaeus got there in an afternoon: the tax-collector who took became, the day salvation entered his house, a man who gave half his goods away (cf. Luke 19:8–9).

For Old Joe, who has never burgled a house in his life, the verse still lands close. Theft wears respectable clothes: the padded expense claim, the hours billed but not worked, the cash job kept off the books, the ‘borrowed’ tools that never find their way home. The command is the same, and so is the surprise: God’s goal for a working life is not merely that it stays honest, but that the pay-packet becomes a channel — that at the end of the month there is margin, on purpose, for the person in need. In Christ, work stops being only how you get and becomes how you give. “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (cf. Acts 20:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sapros — rotten, putrid, the word for decaying food. Speech that tears down, gossips, belittles, or poisons the community is as out of place in the body of Christ as rotting meat at a feast. The standard Paul sets against it is high: every word should be good for building up, fitting the occasion, and — this is the phrase that deserves its own attention — giving grace to those who hear.

What does “that it may give grace to those who hear” mean? Paul is not talking about being polite or pleasant. The word is charis — grace, the same word used throughout Ephesians for God’s undeserved gift. The idea is striking: your words can be a vehicle of grace to another person. Something you say — at the right moment, in the right way — can actually land in someone’s life the way grace lands: undeserved, unexpected, doing something they could not do for themselves. An honest word of encouragement to someone who is doubting. A well-timed truth spoken gently to someone who is drifting. A simple acknowledgement to someone who feels invisible. These are not just nice things to say — they are grace delivered through a human mouth.

The reverse is also true, and Paul implies it. Corrupting talk does not merely fail to give grace — it actively takes it away. A careless word can undo in a moment what months of encouragement built up. A piece of gossip poisons how others see someone before he even walks into the room. A cutting remark at the wrong moment can stay with a person for years. Words have weight in both directions.

A brief example. Two members of a small group hear that a third, James, has just lost his job. The first response: “Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t really cut out for that role.” Possibly true. Zero grace. James is now worse off in the community than before those words were spoken. The second response: “James has just lost his job — he’s really shaken. Could we pray for him now and someone reach out this week?” Same information. Grace given. The body moves toward him rather than past him.

The question Paul sets before every word is not just “is this true?” but “does this build up? Does it fit this moment? Will the person who hears it be richer for it, or poorer?” cf. Prov. 15:23; Col. 4:6.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse arrives like a sudden change of key — and it is meant to. Paul has been speaking about words and community, about the practical texture of life together. And then, without warning, he pulls back the curtain and shows us who is present in the room: the Holy Spirit of God himself, listening to every word, affected by every choice. This is not abstract theology; it is the most personal possible motivation for everything Paul has commanded.

What does it mean to grieve the Holy Spirit? The word Paul uses means to cause grief, to pain, to sadden — the language of deep personal sorrow, the kind felt in close relationships. Paul is not saying the Spirit becomes angry, or that he withdraws his presence, or that the believer loses their salvation. He is saying something more intimate and more searching: the Spirit can be hurt. He is a Person — the third Person of the Trinity — not an impersonal force or a spiritual energy field. He has the full personal attributes of God, including the capacity for relational grief when love is spurned or holiness is violated by those he indwells.

How does grieving the Spirit happen? The context supplies the answer directly. Every command in verses 25–32 describes a way the Spirit can be grieved:

  • Falsehood (v. 25) — the Spirit is the “Spirit of truth” (John 16:13). Every lie spoken among believers grieves the one who is truth’s own advocate.
  • Unresolved anger (vv. 26–27) — the Spirit is the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). Nursing resentment and giving the devil a foothold grieves the one who labours to unite what sin divides.
  • Corrupting speech (v. 29) — the Spirit works to build up the body. Every word that tears down works against him. He hears every conversation in every small group, every comment after the service, every message sent in frustration.
  • Bitterness, wrath, slander, malice (v. 31) — the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Gal. 5:22–23). These vices are the direct opposite of his fruit, and their presence in the community grieves him deeply.

More broadly, the Spirit is grieved whenever a believer treats sin casually, lives as though the old self were still in charge, or refuses the renewal he is working to bring about (vv. 22–24). He is not grieved by weakness, failure, or honest struggle — these he meets with intercession (Rom. 8:26). He is grieved by wilful, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

“By whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — what does this mean? The seal in the ancient world was the mark of ownership and the guarantee of authenticity — pressed into wax on a document or a jar, it said: this belongs to someone, and that someone stands behind it. Paul has already used this image in Ephesians 1:13–14: “you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it.” The Spirit himself is the seal. His presence in the believer is God’s own mark of ownership, God’s guarantee that what he has begun he will complete.

“The day of redemption” is the day of final deliverance — the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the full consummation of all that salvation means. The believer is not yet fully redeemed in experience; the body still groans, sin still remains, the world is still broken. But the seal is already applied. The Spirit’s presence now is the down payment (arrabōn, 1:14 — the first instalment that guarantees the rest) on a redemption that is as certain as God himself.

The argument embedded in “by whom you were sealed” is therefore both a warning and a wonder. The warning: do not grieve the very Person who is your guarantee of glory — who holds your future, who intercedes for you, who applies Christ’s work to your soul day by day. The wonder: the Spirit has not abandoned you despite your griefs. He grieves — and stays. He is sealed to you as surely as you are sealed by him. His grief is the grief of love that will not let go.

cf. Eph. 1:13–14; Isa. 63:10 (“they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit”); Rom. 8:23, 26–27; 2 Cor. 1:22; 1 Thess. 5:19 (“do not quench the Spirit”).

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six words. Paul lines them up like a row of weapons to be laid down — and each one is distinct. Together they describe the full arsenal of a heart that has refused the grace of verse 32. Understanding each term helps the reader see not just the category but the specific thing God is calling them to surrender.

Bitterness — the deep, settled sourness of a soul that has been wounded and has chosen to nurse the wound rather than release it. Bitterness is what anger becomes when it is kept too long. It colours everything: the bitter person reads every new situation through the lens of old pain; they assume the worst, interpret generously toward no one, and carry a weight that poisons not only themselves but everyone around them. Hebrews 12:15 warns of a “root of bitterness” that springs up and “defiles many” — it is never merely personal. Bitterness is always communal in its damage.

Wrath (thymos) — the sudden flare, the hot explosion of passionate anger that erupts and then subsides. Unlike bitterness which is slow and cold, thymos is fast and hot — the flash of temper, the sharp word spoken in a moment of fury, the outburst that leaves wreckage behind. It is the anger that does not think before it speaks. James 1:19–20 addresses it directly: “be slow to anger, for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.”

Anger (orgē) — where thymos is the sudden flare, orgē is the settled, brooding resentment that endures over time. It is the cold version of wrath — deliberate, sustained, often hidden. A person can appear perfectly calm while carrying orgē for years. It is the anger that builds a case, remembers every offence, and waits. Paul has already addressed this in verse 26: do not let the sun go down on it.

Clamour — the loud, public expression of anger: shouting, quarrelling, the raised voice that turns a disagreement into a scene. It is anger that has gone public and lost restraint. In the context of the community Paul is describing, clamour is the moment when a private grievance becomes a public fracture — the argument in the meeting, the confrontation after the service, the email written and sent in heat.

Slander (blasphēmia) — injurious speech about another person: damaging their reputation, speaking evil of them to others, whether the words are true or false. It includes gossip that is factually accurate but maliciously shared, and accusation that goes beyond what is warranted. In its root sense it is the same word used of blasphemy against God — it is speech that defiles and dishonours.
