Slander within the church is a particularly grievous form because it attacks the members of Christ’s body and therefore, in a real sense, Christ himself (cf. Acts 9:4).

Malice — the underlying disposition from which all the others flow: a settled ill-will toward another person, a desire for their harm. It is the soil in which bitterness, wrath, anger, and slander all grow. Paul places it last because it is the root: a person with malice in their heart will find expression for it through all the other vices on the list. The call to put away malice is therefore the most fundamental of the six — it is the call to have the heart itself transformed, not merely the behaviour managed.

And notice the anatomy of the list, for we have seen it before. In verse 18 a hardened heart darkened the understanding and issued at last in a ruined life. Here malice in the heart sours into bitterness, erupts as wrath and anger, and breaks out of the mouth as clamour and slander. Both times the road runs from the heart outward. Both times the cure must begin where the road begins. cf. 1 Pet. 2:1; Col. 3:8.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having stripped the wardrobe bare in verse 31, Paul now furnishes it. Three words — kind, tender-hearted, forgiving — and then the ground on which all three stand: as God in Christ forgave you. This is not a command followed by a standard; it is a command that finds both its power and its pattern in what God has already done.

Kind (chrēstos) — practical, active goodness toward others; a readiness to serve, to meet a need, to go out of one’s way for another person’s benefit. It is the opposite of indifference. The word was used of wine that had mellowed with age — no longer sharp or harsh, but smooth and good. Jesus uses the same root in Matthew 11:30: “my yoke is chrēstos” — easy, gentle, well-fitting. Kindness in Paul’s sense is not merely pleasantness; it is the active disposition that looks for ways to be useful and good to the people around you, especially the difficult ones.

Tender-hearted (eusplagchnos) — literally “good-bowelled” in Greek, the bowels being in ancient thought the seat of deep emotion. It means a heart that is genuinely moved by another person’s pain — not hardened, not professionally sympathetic, but inwardly affected. The tender-hearted person does not manage other people’s suffering from a safe emotional distance; they feel it. This is the compassion of Christ himself, who was repeatedly described as being “moved with compassion” (splagchnizomai, the same root) when he encountered human need (Matt. 9:36; 14:14; Luke 15:20). The opposite of tender-heartedness is the hardness of heart Paul described in verse 18 — the calloused heart that has stopped feeling. The new self, created in God’s likeness, recovers the capacity to be moved.

Forgiving (charizomenoi) — this is the word that carries the full theological weight of the verse. It shares its root with charis — grace. To forgive in Paul’s sense is literally to grace someone: to give them what they do not deserve and cannot earn. It is not the same as excusing (pretending the wrong did not happen), nor is it the same as reconciliation (which requires repentance from the offender and may take time). Forgiveness is a unilateral decision of the will, made by the one who was wronged, to release the debt — to stop holding the offence as a claim, to refuse to let it define the relationship or fuel resentment.

Why is this so hard? Because forgiveness feels like injustice. It feels like letting the other person off the hook, like swallowing a wrong that deserves to be answered. This is why Paul grounds it entirely in the gospel: as God in Christ forgave you. The answer to the injustice objection is the cross. At the cross, the debt was not cancelled by pretending it did not exist; it was absorbed by the one who was wronged. God did not overlook sin; he paid for it himself, in Christ. Christian forgiveness follows the same pattern: you absorb the cost rather than pass it on. You take the loss rather than demand repayment. This is not weakness; it is the most costly and Christlike act a human being can perform. cf. Matt. 18:21–35; Col. 3:13; Luke 23:34.

God as the standard for all three — “as God in Christ forgave you” does not only ground the command to forgive; it sets the standard for all three virtues. God is kind: Romans 2:4 speaks of “the riches of his kindness.” God is tender-hearted: Psalm 103:13 — “as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion.” God forgives: at infinite cost, freely, fully, finally. The Christian is not being asked to find these resources in themselves; they are being asked to pass on what they have already received. The measure of our giving is the measure of what we have been given — and what we have been given is immeasurable.

A practical example. Sarah and a colleague at church, Mark, had a falling out six months ago over a decision made in the worship team. Mark handled it badly — he was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others, and never apologised. Sarah has been cold toward him since; she serves alongside him on Sunday mornings but keeps her distance, responds to his messages with minimum courtesy, and has told two friends what happened. She tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day.

Paul’s three words expose where she actually is. The kindness is gone — she has stopped looking for ways to serve or encourage Mark. The tender-heartedness has closed down — she does not want to know how he is doing. And the forgiveness is incomplete: she has released the acute pain but retained the verdict. The coolness, the strategic distance, the quiet word to two friends — these are the residue of an unforgiven debt still being held.

The way forward is not a feeling but a decision — made in prayer, grounded in the cross: Lord, I release this. Mark owes me nothing. I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I extend the same. Then the behaviour follows the decision: a genuine word toward Mark, an end to the quiet commentary to friends, a willingness to be present rather than managed. It will not feel natural immediately. It may need to be made again tomorrow. But this is what it looks like to live verse 32 in a real community, in a real week, with a real person who hurt you and never said sorry.

And this is where the whole chapter has been going. The old clothes come off, the mind is renewed, the new clothes go on — not so that we may admire ourselves in them, but because God has set his heart on presenting his people to himself “in splendour, without spot or wrinkle… holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5:27). Every truthful word, every anger surrendered before sundown, every hand that gives instead of takes, every debt released — these are the bride being made ready. He is not merely tidying our behaviour. He is dressing a bride for the day she sees her Husband’s face. cf. Eph. 5:25–27; Rev. 19:7–8.

4.theology:
Ephesians 4 stakes out the great Reformed doctrine of the inseparability of justification and sanctification. The same grace that declares the sinner righteous also begins to make them righteous. Not simultaneously, not automatically — but inevitably. Where the root is real, the fruit will come. Paul’s commands in this chapter are not the conditions of acceptance; they are the evidence of it. The indicative always precedes and grounds the imperative.

The chapter also gives the church its most searching doctrine of common life. The body of Christ is not a collection of private spiritual journeys happening in the same building. It is an organism, with every member genuinely joined to every other — responsible for each other’s growth, dependent on each other’s gifts, harmed by each other’s sin. Falsehood in the body is not a private failure; it is a systemic wound. Unresolved anger is not a personal problem; it is a strategic opening for the enemy. This is the doctrine of the church made viscerally practical.

And at the centre stands the renewal of the mind — the hinge on which all change turns. Not willpower, not behaviour management, but transformation at the level where thinking happens. This is the Spirit’s sovereign work, received through the ordinary means of grace: the word, prayer, honest community, and obedience to what is already known. The Christian does not renew themselves. But they can position themselves daily in the hands of the One who does. cf. Rom. 12:1–2; 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.
4.examples:
Then: The Ephesian believers had come out of a culture saturated with the very patterns Paul describes in vv. 17–19 — a world of mystery religions, sexual licence, and moral relativism where the only sin was public embarrassment. To be told to “put off” this was not a minor adjustment; it was a complete reorientation of identity. And the alternative Paul offered — speaking truth, controlling anger, working honestly, forgiving freely — would have looked countercultural to the point of strangeness. The church in Ephesus was being asked to be a visible sign that a different humanity was possible.

Now: The culture has changed; the pressure has not. The same patterns Paul named are alive and well: the mind drifting, the conscience growing quieter, the appetite demanding more. The same temptations assault the same pressure points: to manage rather than truth-tell, to nurse grievance rather than forgive, to speak what entertains rather than what builds. And the same command stands: no longer walk as those who do not know God. Not because you must earn your standing — that is secured in Christ — but because you have been made new, and new creatures do not live in the old way.

Old Joe reading this chapter on Monday morning can take one thing to work: the person sitting across from him is either a fellow member of the body or a neighbour made in God’s image. Either way, what he says matters, what he does with his anger matters, how he handles the truth matters. The renewal of the mind is not a mystical event. It is what happens when the Christian opens the Bible instead of the phone, prays instead of broods, speaks the honest word instead of the comfortable one — and does it again tomorrow. This is how the body builds itself up in love.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.” The command is breathtaking in its scope, and its motivation is everything. We imitate God not because he is powerful or sovereign or even just — but because we are his beloved children, and children naturally, joyfully imitate those who love them. The motivation for holy living is not duty but delight, not fear but love, not the dread of punishment but the joy of resemblance.

The specific attribute to be imitated is love — but immediately defined by the cross: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, “a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (v. 2). This phrase reaches deep into the Old Testament sacrificial system. The “fragrant offering” (reah nichoach) was the language of divine acceptance — from Genesis 8:21 through the Levitical offerings, whenever God declared himself pleased with the sacrifice. Christ’s self-giving is the final, fully accepted offering that all those animal sacrifices could only foreshadow: freely given (prosphora) and enormously costly (thysia). The Father smells the fragrance and is satisfied. Wrath propitiated, covenant restored, the guilty declared righteous. This is the love to be imitated: cross-shaped, self-giving, asking not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need and what will it cost me to give it?”

Against this backdrop Paul names what does not belong: sexual immorality (porneia — the full range of sexual activity outside the marriage covenant; sex as a covenant act mirroring Christ and the church, too sacred to be treated as casual), impurity (akatharsia — broader than overt act, covering the imagination and desire not yet expressed; the inner life matters to God as much as the outer), and covetousness (pleonexia — the insatiable craving for more, the desire that places a created thing in the throne that belongs to God alone, which is why Paul calls it idolatry in v. 5). Covetousness must be distinguished from wise stewardship: providing for a household, prudent financial planning, and enjoying God’s good gifts are not covetousness. The diagnostic questions are: what is driving it? where is the heart set? does it produce generosity or hoarding? The root of covetousness is a failure of trust — a rival religion, the worship of More in place of the God who is enough.

The warning of verses 5–6 is sobering — those who practice these things without repentance have no inheritance in the kingdom. But a pastoral word is essential: Paul is describing a settled, unrepentant pattern of life, not the experience of the believer who struggles, falls, grieves, and returns. The evidence of genuine faith is not the absence of struggle but the presence of grief over sin and the refusal to make peace with what Christ died to remove. The dangerous condition is not the fall but the cessation of struggle — listening to the “empty words” of v. 6 and reclassifying sin as not-sin. For the one who is genuinely fighting: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). A bruised reed he will not break (Isa. 42:3).
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

"A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of His people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ Himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: "Be imitators of God" — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The mystery religions and philosophical schools both spoke of homoiōsis theō — likeness to God — as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave Himself up, who went to the cross for His enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured Himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave His Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants His children to look like Him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mimētai tou theou — imitators of God. The Greek word gives us “mime.” A child mimics a parent in play; the grown child imitates a father in earnest. This is Paul’s call — not to copy a set of rules but to watch the Father and do likewise.

The ground of the command is everything: “as beloved children”. We imitate God not to earn his favour but because we already have it. The motivation is love received, not performance demanded. A child who is secure in a father’s love naturally wants to be like him. That is the dynamic Paul is describing. cf. Matt. 5:48; 1 John 3:1–3.

verseByVerse.quote: And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The standard of love is the cross. Christ loved us and gave himself up — voluntarily, at infinite personal cost, for our benefit and not his own. This is the pattern. Not sentiment, not natural affection, but cross-shaped love that asks not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need, and what will it cost me to give it?”

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” — what did Paul mean? He is reaching into the deep language of the Old Testament sacrificial system. A “fragrant offering” (rêah nicôach in Hebrew) was the phrase used when God declared himself pleased with a sacrifice — when the offering was accepted, the worshipper received. It runs through Leviticus and Numbers for the burnt and peace offerings, appearing first at Noah’s altar after the flood (Gen. 8:21). It is the language of divine acceptance: the sacrifice has reached God, God is satisfied, the relationship is right.

Paul applies this whole weight to the cross. Every animal sacrifice in Israel’s history was pointing toward this one moment — foreshadowing the real thing. Where repeated sacrifices could never finally deal with sin (Heb. 10:1–4), Christ’s offering was the one, fully accepted, once-for-all sacrifice: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Heb. 10:14). The Father smelled the fragrance and was satisfied. The wrath was absorbed. The broken relationship was restored.

Two words deepen the picture. Prosphora (offering) stresses the voluntariness — Christ was not seized; he gave himself (John 10:18). Thysia (sacrifice) stresses the cost — the actual giving of life. Together: freely given and enormously costly. Neither can be separated from the other.

This is what Paul holds before us as the pattern for how we are to love one another. The cross is not only the ground of our salvation; it is the shape of our lives. cf. John 13:34; 1 John 3:16; Heb. 10:1–14; Rom. 3:25.

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three vices — sexual immorality (porneia), impurity (akatharsia), covetousness (pleonexia) — are not merely to be avoided but not even named, not entering the vocabulary or the imagination of the community. “As is proper among saints” — the standard is identity, not merely morality. Saints are holy people, set apart; what defiles has no place in the set-apart community. Paul will name covetousness as idolatry in v. 5: the craving for more — whether sexual pleasure or material possession — is ultimately the worship of a false god placed in the seat that belongs to the Creator alone.

Sexual immorality (porneia) — the Greek word is broad: it covers every form of sexual activity outside the covenant of marriage between a man and a woman. This includes pre-marital sex, adultery, pornography (a word that shares the same root), and any sexual conduct that removes intimacy from the covenantal relationship for which God designed it. Paul is not addressing edge cases; he is naming the whole category. The reason is not that the body is evil — it is not; it is created by God and redeemed by Christ (1 Cor. 6:19–20) — but that sexual union is so powerful, so deep, and so image-bearing that to misuse it is to damage something at the core of what it means to be human. Sex in Scripture is not primarily about pleasure (though pleasure is a genuine gift within it); it is a physical covenant act that mirrors the union between Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32). To treat it as a casual transaction is to desecrate a sacrament. cf. 1 Cor. 6:18–20; 1 Thess. 4:3–5.

Impurity (akatharsia) — already defined at 4:19, but worth noting here that Paul places it alongside porneia to show it is broader than overt sexual sin. It covers the whole range of moral defilement: corrupt desire, fantasy, the imagination fed on what is degrading, the mind that entertains what the hands do not yet do. Jesus made this point in Matthew 5:28: the look of lust is already the act in the heart. Akatharsia catches what porneia might miss: the inner life of desire that has not yet expressed itself in action but is already corrupted. A person can avoid every outward act and still be deeply impure in their thought-life — and Paul says that too has no place among the saints.

Covetousness (pleonexia) — literally “the desire to have more” (pleon = more, echein = to have). It is the insatiable craving for more than you have — more money, more status, more possessions, more comfort, more pleasure — driven not by need but by an appetite that cannot be satisfied. Paul has already used this word at 4:19 for the Gentile condition: “greedy to practice every kind of impurity.” Here he places it alongside sexual sin because the underlying dynamic is the same: both are forms of wanting what God has not given, taking what does not belong to you, and placing a craving in the throne of the heart that belongs to God alone. This is why Paul calls it idolatry in verse 5: the covetous person has made their desire their god.

The difference between covetousness and good stewardship or planning — this is an important distinction, and Scripture is careful to maintain it. Covetousness is not the same as:

  • Providing for your household. 1 Timothy 5:8 says that a person who does not provide for their family “has denied the faith.” Earning, saving, and planning for those in your care is not covetousness; it is faithfulness.
  • Wise financial planning. Proverbs 6:6–8 commends the ant who stores provision in summer for winter. Joseph stored grain for seven years against seven years of famine (Gen. 41). Prudent stewardship of what God has given — budgeting, saving, investing for future need — is not covetousness; it is wisdom.
  • Enjoying God’s good gifts. 1 Timothy 6:17 instructs the rich “not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.” Delight in good things — a home, beauty, a meal, a holiday — is not covetousness; it is gratitude.
  • Legitimate ambition. Working hard, developing skills, seeking promotion, building a business — none of these is covetousness in itself. The desire to do excellent work and be rewarded for it is not the same as an insatiable craving for more.

The diagnostic questions that distinguish covetousness from stewardship are these:

  • What is driving it? Stewardship is driven by love for God and others, a sense of responsibility for what God has entrusted. Covetousness is driven by an appetite that is never satisfied — the person who earns more and is still restless, who upgrades and is immediately eyeing the next upgrade, who compares what they have with what others have and feels diminished.
  • Where is the heart set? Matthew 6:21: “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” The steward holds money and possessions as a trust from God, open-handed, ready to give generously. The covetous person holds them with a closed fist — they define security, identity, and worth. Losing them is not inconvenience but devastation.
  • Does it produce generosity or hoarding? The steward who plans well also gives well — 2 Corinthians 9:6–8: “whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully… God loves a cheerful giver.” Covetousness produces the opposite: the more accumulated, the harder it becomes to release any of it. cf. Luke 12:15–21 (the rich fool who planned well but lived for himself and was a fool toward God).

The root of covetousness, ultimately, is a failure of trust: the belief, however unconscious, that God cannot be relied upon to provide, that security must be seized rather than received, that having more will finally deliver the peace that God alone can give. This is why Paul calls it idolatry. It is not merely greed; it is a rival religion — the worship of More in place of the God who is enough. cf. Phil. 4:11–13; Heb. 13:5; Luke 12:15.

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary: The catalog moves from deeds to words: filthiness, foolish talk, crude joking. The Greco-Roman world celebrated wit and bawdy humor; Paul marks it as “out of place” in the community of the cross. The antidote is striking: not solemn silence but thanksgiving. Gratitude is the natural speech of those who know what they have been given. A heart full of genuine thanksgiving has no room for talk that degrades; it overflows with praise. The same Greek word (eucharistia, thanksgiving) gives us “Eucharist” — the name many Christian traditions use for the Lord’s Supper or Communion, the meal of remembrance and thanksgiving at the heart of Christian worship. The connection is deliberate: the table where we remember what Christ gave us is meant to shape everything we say away from that table. A mouth full of genuine gratitude for the cross has little room left for the words Paul just listed.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the theological root of his warnings: sexual immorality and covetousness are not merely moral failures — they are idolatry. The covetous person has made possession their god; the sexually immoral person has made pleasure their god. Both are worship directed at the wrong object, and Paul calls it by its right name. cf. Rom. 1:25; Col. 3:5.

“Has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” — what does this mean? The inheritance is the full possession of the kingdom at the last day — the resurrection life, the new creation, the unhindered presence of God, everything that Christ secured for his people. To have no inheritance there is to be excluded from all of it. This is Paul’s most solemn language: not a warning about lesser blessing, but about being outside the kingdom entirely. The people he is describing — the sexually immoral, the impure, the covetous as a settled way of life — are not the citizens of that kingdom. Their allegiance, their worship, their identity belong elsewhere.

But many true believers struggle with exactly these sins — does this mean they are not saved? This is the question that must be answered carefully and biblically, because the pastoral stakes are high. Two truths must be held together.

First, Paul is describing a pattern of life, not a moment of failure. The Greek participles are present and ongoing: the person who is sexually immoral, who is covetous — as a settled, unrepentant, unchallengeable way of living. He is not describing the believer who falls, grieves, confesses, and fights. He is describing the person for whom these things are simply who they are — untroubled, unrepentant, with no war being waged. 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 makes the same point and then adds: “and such were some of you.” Past tense. That is the key. The person who has truly come to Christ has been washed, sanctified, justified. Their direction has changed, even if the struggle has not ended.

Second, the presence of the struggle is itself the evidence of new life. The person who falls into sexual sin and is devastated, who fights covetousness and hates it in themselves, who longs to be free — that person is not the one Paul is warning. The unregenerate person does not wage war against their sin; they make peace with it. Romans 7 describes the genuine believer as someone who cries out: “wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me?” That cry of anguish is not the voice of the kingdom-excluded. It is the voice of someone who belongs to Christ and knows it — and knows they are not yet what they will be.

The sharp biblical distinction is this: the mark of the unbeliever is not that they sin, but that they do not fight. The mark of the believer is not that they never fall, but that they cannot stay down — they confess, they return, they hate what they do and love what they want to become. If you are troubled by this verse, that trouble is itself a sign of life. The person Paul is warning is not troubled at all. cf. 1 Cor. 6:9–11; Rom. 7:24–8:1; 1 John 1:8–9; 3:9.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Empty words” are the sophistries of those who minimise the stakes: “God is gracious; these things don’t really matter;” “everyone struggles with this;” “a loving God would not judge.” Paul calls them lies. These are the very things for which God’s wrath falls on the sons of disobedience — not arbitrary punishment but the settled, holy opposition of the righteous God to all that destroys his image-bearers and dishonours his name.

A pastoral word for the struggling believer. Someone reading verses 5–6 may feel the ground give way beneath them. They know their own heart. They struggle with sexual temptation — perhaps seriously, persistently, with repeated failure. Or they recognise the covetousness Paul names and know it runs deep in them. And now they read: no inheritance in the kingdom. Is that me? Am I lost?

This passage must be read with great care, and with the whole of Scripture in view. Paul is not writing to people who struggle with these sins; he is writing to people who practice them without repentance, who have given themselves over to them as a way of life, whose identity is defined by them — what he calls elsewhere “the sons of disobedience” (v. 6; cf. 2:2). The Greek word for “everyone who is” in verse 5 refers to a settled, characterising practice — not a battle, but a surrender.

The distinction Scripture draws is not between the sinless and the sinful — there are no sinless people this side of glory — but between those who are walking in the light and those who are walking in darkness (1 John 1:5–9). The person who struggles with sexual temptation, who falls and is grieved by it, who confesses and returns, who hates the sin and longs to be free of it — that person is not described by verse 5. They are described by 1 John 1:9: “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

The evidence of genuine faith is not the absence of struggle but the presence of grief over sin, the ongoing desire for holiness, and the refusal to make peace with what Christ died to remove. The genuine believer does not look at their sin and say “this is fine.” They look at it and say “this is not who I am in Christ — Lord, deliver me.” That cry is itself the mark of the Spirit’s work. Romans 7 — the anguished “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate” (v. 15) — is not the cry of an unbeliever; it is the cry of a person in whom the new self and the old self are genuinely at war. The war is the evidence of life.

What Paul is warning against is something different: the person who has stopped fighting. Who has reclassified their sin as not-sin, who has listened to the “empty words” of verse 6 and settled into a pattern of unrepentant practice while maintaining a Christian identity. That is the dangerous condition — not the struggle, but the cessation of struggle; not the fall, but the refusal to get up.

If you are reading this and you are struggling — genuinely struggling, grieved, wanting to be free — hear the word that stands over all of Paul’s warnings: “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). The blood of Christ is sufficient for every sin you have committed and every sin you will commit. The Spirit who grieves over your sin (4:30) is also the one who intercedes for you with groanings too deep for words (Rom. 8:26). You are not beyond reach. You are not abandoned. Keep fighting. Keep confessing. Keep returning. cf. 1 John 1:8–9; Rom. 8:1; Ps. 51:17; Isa. 42:3 (“a bruised reed he will not break”).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary: “Therefore” draws the conclusion from the gravity of vv. 5–6: because these works bring wrath, and because the community belongs to the kingdom of light (v. 8), a clear distinction must be maintained. “Do not become partners” — do not enter fellowship or complicity in these works. This is not an instruction to social isolation from unbelievers but a refusal to participate in the practices that belong to the old age. The church cannot be the church and also share in the works of darkness without fundamental self-contradiction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." The sharpness of this contrast arrests us every time we read it. Not "you were in darkness" — you were darkness itself. Not "you are now in the light" — you are light. The transformation is total, ontological, irreversible. Something has changed at the deepest level of what you are, not merely where you are or what you do. And the imperative that follows — "walk as children of light" — is not a command to achieve something new but to express something already true. Be in your behaviour what you are in your nature. Let the outside match the inside.

Light bears fruit. The fruit of light is "in all goodness and righteousness and truth" (v.9) — three qualities that together describe the character of the God who is light (1 John 1:5). The child of light is not defined primarily by what they avoid but by what they produce: genuine moral goodness, the rightness of life aligned with God's law and character, the transparency of truth-telling in every dimension of life. This fruit is not manufactured by effort; it grows naturally from a nature that has been fundamentally changed. Light cannot help but produce light-fruits.

And light exposes what darkness conceals. The children of light do not retreat from the darkness of the culture (withdrawal) or blend into it (accommodation). They expose it — by the simple, consistent, visible presence of a life lived in the open before God. This exposure is not aggressive or confrontational; it does not require denunciation or political engagement (though these may have their place). It requires holiness. "When anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible" (v.13). The most prophetic thing the church can do in a dark age is simply to be genuinely, visibly, persistently light.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — "you were darkness," "you are light" — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to "take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them" (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — "the things they do in secret" — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: "Awake, O sleeper" has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul does not say they were in darkness and are now in light. He says they were darkness and are light — a change of nature, not merely of location. The very substance of what they are has been transformed by union with Christ. “Walk as children of light” — the indicative becomes the imperative. You do not walk in the light to become light; you walk as light because you already are light in the Lord.

But what does Paul actually mean by “darkness” and “light” here? He is not talking about ignorance and knowledge in a general sense, as if education is the answer. These are moral and spiritual categories, and they run deep in Scripture.

Darkness, in Paul’s use, means a life orientated away from God — the condition of the soul that has no living connection to him. It is not merely doing wrong things; it is being in the wrong direction entirely. In darkness, the moral compass does not work: what is evil looks acceptable, what is shameful is done without shame (v. 12), what is false feels true. Darkness is the natural habitat of the old self Paul described in chapter 4 — the hardened heart, the calloused conscience, the insatiable appetite. It is the domain where the “rulers and authorities” of 6:12 operate. And before Christ, Paul says bluntly: you were not merely in it — you were it.

Light is the opposite in every dimension. It means a life now orientated toward God — connected to him, defined by him, reflecting him. In Scripture, God himself is light (1 John 1:5: “God is light and in him is no darkness at all”). Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12). To be light in the Lord is to share in his nature, to have the moral compass restored, to be able to see truly — what is good, what is right, what is true (v. 9). It means the things that flourish in darkness — shame, deception, hidden sin — cannot survive in you the way they once did, because light exposes them.

For Old Joe: darkness is not just “being bad.” It is being without God, in a condition where you cannot even see clearly enough to know how lost you are. Light is not just “being better.” It is being joined to the One who is light, so that his nature begins to show in yours. The change Paul is describing is not moral improvement — it is a new identity. cf. John 1:4–5; 1 John 1:5–7; Col. 1:13.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parenthesis defines what light naturally produces: goodness (moral excellence), righteousness (right relating to others), and truth (integrity, correspondence with reality). These three are not rules to perform but fruit to bear — the natural produce of a life transformed into light.

“Try to discern” — is this really the original text? Yes. The Greek verb is dokimazein — to test, to examine, to approve after careful evaluation. It is the word used for assaying metal to determine whether it is genuine. And it is worth pausing on, because Paul normally issues direct commands. Do this. Stop that. Put off. Put on. But here he does not say “obey this list” or “follow these rules.” He says: discern.

Why? Because the Christian life cannot be reduced to a rulebook. Rules cover the cases the lawmaker anticipated. Life constantly produces situations no rulebook has addressed. What Paul is calling for here is something deeper than compliance — it is the cultivated ability to read a situation in the light of knowing Christ and ask: what would please him here? This requires a mind that has been renewed (4:23), a conscience that is sensitive to the Spirit, and a growing knowledge of what God values. It is, in short, wisdom — which is exactly what the next section (vv. 15–17) is about.

The word dokimazein also appears in Romans 12:2: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.” The same logic: the renewed mind does not just follow instructions — it develops the capacity to perceive. Paul is describing moral maturity, not moral compliance. The goal is not a Christian who does right because they were told to, but one who has been so formed by Christ that they can see what is right for themselves. cf. Phil. 1:9–10: “that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent.”

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Unfruitful works of darkness” — fruitlessness is the mark of the old life; where the fruit of light is good, right, and true, the works of darkness bear nothing that survives. The command is not only to abstain but to expose — rebuke, convict, bring into the open. This does not require lurid description; v. 12 notes that what is done in secret is too shameful even to name. Exposure happens through contrast: the sheer presence of lives lived in light makes darkness visible without needing to enumerate its contents in detail.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The logic is arresting: when light exposes darkness, the exposed thing becomes light — transformed by the very exposure that reveals it. This describes both the conversion of sinners (their sin brought into the open by the gospel, they are transformed) and the purification of the community (sins dealt with openly are healed).

A plain example for Old Joe. Think of a believer who has been carrying a hidden sin for years — something they have never told anyone. The weight of it has not gone away; it has grown. The moment they finally bring it into the light — confessing it to God, to a trusted friend, to a pastor — something unexpected happens: the grip of that sin weakens. Not because the confession is magic, but because light has entered where darkness had been living undisturbed. The shame decreases; freedom to draw near to God returns; healing begins. This is Paul’s point: the exposure itself is not just an unmasking; it is the beginning of transformation. Light does not merely reveal — it changes what it touches.

The hymn fragment of v. 14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is almost certainly a quotation, introduced by Paul’s “for it says”, the same formula used to introduce OT Scripture (e.g., 4:8; 5:14). But the words do not appear verbatim anywhere in the OT. Preachers should explain the three possibilities: (1) An OT conflation: the words draw on Isaiah 26:19 (“Your dead shall live… awake and sing for joy”) and Isaiah 60:1 (“Arise, shine, for your light has come”) — Paul weaves the two resurrection-and-light passages together. (2) An early Christian baptismal hymn (the majority modern scholarly view — Lincoln, Fee, Thielman): this was a hymn fragment sung in the primitive church, possibly at baptisms, where the one being baptized was called to “arise” from the waters as from death, into the light of Christ. Paul cites it as authoritative early Christian confession. (3) A lost apocryphal source: the Father Epiphanius attributed these words to an “Apocalypse of Elijah”; modern scholars regard this as unlikely. The most defensible reading: Paul quotes a Spirit-inspired early church hymn that itself distills OT resurrection-and-light imagery, and applies it as an evangelistic call to the sleeper who has not yet risen into Christ’s light. The text is a call to conversion expressed through the language of resurrection — the same language Paul has been using for salvation throughout the letter (2:1–6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil." The third walk imperative carries a quality of urgency that is eschatological in character. The Christian does not live in a neutral moment; they live in a moment freighted with significance, in days that are evil (and therefore time-limited in their evil), in a window of opportunity that will not remain open forever. Wisdom means seeing this clearly and acting accordingly — not frantic and anxious, but alert and intentional, making the most of every opportunity because the Kingdom has come and its King is returning.

The contrast Paul draws between drunkenness and fullness of the Spirit is one of the most theologically provocative contrasts in the letter. He is not simply contrasting vice and virtue, or bad behaviour and good. He is contrasting two kinds of fullness — two ways of trying to transcend the ordinary, to escape the limitations of sober consciousness, to find ecstasy. Wine offers dissolution — the loss of self, the blurring of edges, the temporary escape from sobriety into sensation. The Spirit offers something entirely different: not the loss of self but the fullness of self as God intended it, overflowing with a joy that is oriented outward, that expresses itself in song and gratitude and the mutual submission that makes genuine community possible.

The Spirit-filled life Paul describes is intensely communal in its expression. It erupts in singing — "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (v.19) — a rich triad suggesting the full range of musical and devotional expression available to the church. It issues in "giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" — a gratitude so comprehensive that nothing is excluded from its scope. And it produces "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" — the mutual humility that Paul will apply to marriage, family, and household in the verses that follow. The Spirit-filled community looks and sounds different from the world around it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

"Be filled with the Spirit" (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. Calvin wrote that the Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and that the asking must be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. The Reformed tradition has generally understood the Psalms as the divinely given hymnal of the church, with "hymns and spiritual songs" expanding the range of legitimate worship expression. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who "did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself" (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The worship of Artemis and the mystery religions of Ephesus were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness He gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God Himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Look carefully” — precise, deliberate attention to the direction of one’s life. The contrast is wise versus unwise — wisdom being the God-given capacity to see life as God sees it and live accordingly. Exagorazomenoi ton kairon — “buying up the time,” redeeming the opportunity. Kairos is not clock time but the critical moment, the opportunity that may not come again. “The days are evil” — the present age is morally compromised and hostile to the things of God. Precisely because the environment is dangerous and the opportunities precious, the believer must move through time with costly intention.

A brief illustration. A surgeon does not walk into an operating theatre the way she walks into a supermarket. In the theatre she is acutely aware of what is at stake, what each moment requires, what a small misjudgement could cost. She is not anxious — she is trained and focused. She moves deliberately because the situation demands it.

Paul is asking the Christian to bring that same quality of attention to the whole of life. Not anxiety, but wakefulness. Not frantic busyness, but the refusal to drift. The days are evil — which means the current is flowing against you. A boat on a river with a strong current does not stay still by doing nothing; it drifts downstream. Staying where you should be, let alone moving forward, requires active, deliberate effort.

For Old Joe: this verse is a quiet warning against the kind of life that just happens — where the years pass and the opportunities to pray, to speak a word for Christ, to serve, to invest in someone’s faith, simply slip by unconsidered. The unwise person does not make a dramatic decision to waste their life; they simply never make the decision not to. cf. Col. 4:5; Ps. 90:12: “teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.”

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Foolish” — without moral understanding — is the opposite of the wisdom urged in vv. 15–16. The antidote is not more information but understanding — grasping with the mind and living from that grasp — of what the will of the Lord is. This is the great orienting question of the wise life: not what is convenient, what is acceptable, what everyone else is doing — but what does the Lord want here? This understanding comes through Scripture, Spirit, and the counsel of the community, and it becomes the steering mechanism of the redeemed life.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast is not arbitrary. Wine was central to the ecstatic cults of Ephesus — intoxication as the path to spiritual experience, the self surrendered to an external power. Paul refuses the counterfeit: not wine (in which is asōtia — dissolution, the self without restraint) but the Spirit. “Be filled” is continuous and receptive — ongoing, kept happening by the Spirit’s action not your effort. You do not fill yourself; you position yourself to be filled. And what follows immediately (vv. 19–21) is entirely relational: Spirit-filling is not private mystical experience but community transformation. (cf. Acts 2:4; Col. 3:16)

What does being filled with the Spirit actually mean? The image of filling implies both capacity and control. To be filled with something is to be dominated, directed, and energised by it — the way a sail is filled with wind, or a vessel with water. Paul is not describing a second blessing received once and retained permanently, nor an ecstatic experience detached from ordinary life. Plērousthe is present continuous: keep being filled, again and again, as an ongoing reality of the Christian life. The believer who was filled yesterday needs to be filled again today. It is less like a reservoir that is topped up once and more like breathing — a continuous, vital, daily dependence.

To be filled with the Spirit means that the Spirit, who already indwells every believer (Rom. 8:9; 1 Cor. 6:19), is given full control — that his priorities, not the flesh’s, set the agenda; that his power, not human effort, drives the life; that his fruit (Gal. 5:22–23) is visibly ripening. It is the Spirit operating at full capacity in the space the believer opens to him, rather than being grieved (4:30) or quenched (1 Thess. 5:19) by sin, self-reliance, or neglect.

What can the believer do — or stop doing? Scripture does not give a formula, but it is clear that certain things grieve and quench the Spirit while others open the life to his filling:

What to stop:

  • Stop grieving the Spirit through unconfessed sin (4:30). Sin does not remove the Spirit from the believer, but it hinders his free operation. Unconfessed, unrepented sin is like a hand on the valve. Confession and repentance reopen the flow. 1 John 1:9 is the practical key: keep short accounts with God.
  • Stop quenching the Spirit (1 Thess. 5:19). To quench is to damp down a fire — to suppress the Spirit’s promptings, to ignore his convictions, to silence his nudges toward obedience, witness, or prayer. The believer who repeatedly ignores the Spirit’s promptings trains themselves to hear him less clearly over time.
  • Stop filling the space with substitutes. Paul’s contrast with wine is deliberate: the person who numbs themselves with entertainment, distraction, busyness, or any form of intoxication — however socially acceptable — is filling the space the Spirit is meant to fill. The question is not only “what am I doing?” but “what is filling my inner life?”

What to do:

  • Ask. Luke 11:13: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” This is the simplest and most overlooked means. The Christian who begins each day with “Father, fill me with your Spirit today” is not performing a ritual — they are making the fundamental acknowledgement that they cannot live the Christian life under their own power, and inviting the One who can.
  • Immerse yourself in Scripture. Colossians 3:16 — “let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” — is the parallel passage to this verse, and what follows is almost identical to what follows here (singing, thankfulness, mutual submission). The Spirit works through the word. A life saturated in Scripture is a life open to the Spirit’s filling in a way that a word-starved life simply is not.
  • Worship. Verses 19–20 show that Spirit-filling immediately overflows into song, gratitude, and the glorifying of God. But this works in both directions: deliberate, wholehearted worship — not as performance but as the genuine lifting of the heart to God — is itself a means of opening to the Spirit. The person who worships regularly, honestly, and with attention to who God is, cultivates a receptivity to the Spirit that forms over time.
  • Obey the prompting you already have. The Spirit gives light for the next step, not a map of the whole journey. The believer who acts on the conviction already given — the apology to make, the word to speak, the sin to confess, the person to serve — finds the Spirit faithful and their capacity for his direction grows. Obedience is the posture of the filled life. cf. John 14:21: “whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me… and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”
  • Stay in community. The filling of the Spirit in this passage is explicitly communal in its outcome (vv. 19–21). The believer who withdraws from the body cuts themselves off from one of the Spirit’s primary means of working. Regular gathering, honest fellowship, and the mutual ministry of the body are not optional additions to the Spirit-filled life; they are part of its ordinary environment.

To what end is the Spirit filling? Verses 19–21 answer immediately. The Spirit-filled life does not turn inward; it turns outward and upward. It produces:

  • Worship — psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; the heart making melody to the Lord (v. 19). The first evidence of the Spirit’s filling is not a private experience but a song rising to God.
  • Thankfulness — “giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 20). The filled believer sees the hand of God in all things and responds with gratitude rather than complaint.
  • Mutual submission — “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (v. 21). The Spirit does not fill a person and make them more impressive or more dominant; he fills them and makes them more servant-hearted. Every relationship that follows in chapters 5–6 (husband and wife, parent and child, master and servant) flows from this verse. Spirit-filling is not mystical height; it is relational depth and servanthood in the ordinary places of life.

The Spirit-filled life is therefore not primarily characterised by extraordinary experiences but by an ordinary life made extraordinary from the inside: full of worship, full of gratitude, full of self-giving love — the very character of Christ reproduced in his people by his Spirit. cf. Gal. 5:22–23; Acts 4:31; Col. 3:16–17.

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit-filled life overflows in song and thanksgiving. Three types of song — psalms (the OT Psalter, the church’s permanent hymnbook), hymns (focused doxology), spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted expression) — fill the community’s common life. “Addressing one another” — worship is mutual and horizontal as well as vertical; believers build one another up in song. “Making melody to the Lord with your heart” — the music is not performance but from the heart. “Giving thanks always and for everything” — the scope is total: always, for everything, because God the Father is sovereign and Jesus Christ is the mediator of every blessing.

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — what did Paul mean? This phrase is one of the most frequently used in Christian prayer and worship, and one of the least examined. It is not a verbal formula appended to prayers to make them valid — a kind of password that unlocks divine attention. To understand what Paul means, the phrase must be unpacked from its biblical roots.

In Scripture, a person’s name stands for their whole person — their character, their authority, their identity, everything they are. To act “in someone’s name” in the ancient world was to act as their authorised representative, on their behalf, in their authority. An ambassador speaks in the name of the king — not meaning he mentions the king’s name in every sentence, but that he stands before the receiving court with the king’s full backing and speaks with his authority. cf. Col. 3:17: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.”

To give thanks “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” therefore carries at least three distinct and weighty meanings:

  • Through Christ as mediator. The believer has no standing before God the Father in themselves. We are sinners; God is holy. The only reason our thanksgiving reaches the Father at all is that it is offered through the one Mediator between God and humanity (1 Tim. 2:5) — the Lord Jesus Christ, who by his blood has opened the way into the Father’s presence (Eph. 2:18; Heb. 10:19–22). To give thanks in his name is to acknowledge that every act of worship is possible only because of the cross. The most ordinary prayer of gratitude — “thank you, Father, for this meal” — rests on the atonement.
  • On the authority of Christ. The believer approaches the Father not as a stranger or a subject petitioning a distant king, but as a child of the household, admitted by Christ’s own invitation: “until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16:24). To pray and give thanks in his name is to come with the full weight of Christ’s merit behind the approach — not our worthiness but his, not our track record but his perfect obedience presented to the Father on our behalf.
  • In alignment with Christ’s character and purposes. “In the name of Jesus” is not a blank cheque. It means giving thanks and praying in a way that is consistent with who Jesus is and what he is doing in the world — aligned with his will, shaped by his priorities, directed toward his glory. John 14:13–14: “whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” The goal is the Father’s glory in the Son — which means that thanksgiving offered “in his name” is thanksgiving that acknowledges God as the source of every blessing and him alone as worthy of the praise.

Taken together: when the believer gives thanks to God the Father in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, they are doing something of profound theological weight in the simplest act. They are approaching the Father through the Mediator who purchased their access, with the authority Christ has granted them as his brothers and sisters, in a spirit aligned with his own purposes and glory. The phrase is the entire gospel compressed into a posture of gratitude. cf. John 14:6; Rom. 1:8; Heb. 13:15 (“through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God”).

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is the hinge between the Spirit-filled life (vv. 18–20) and the household code (vv. 22–6:9). “Submitting to one another” — mutual submission is the atmosphere of the Spirit-filled community; each person placing the other above themselves. “Out of reverence for Christ” makes Christ, not social convention, the motive for every submissive relationship. The household code that follows is not a baptism of Greco-Roman social structures but an application of this Christ-governed mutual submission to the concrete realities of household life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the Spirit-filled community of mutual submission (v. 21), Paul descends into the most intimate community of all — marriage — and what he finds there is not merely a domestic arrangement to be governed by wise principles but a living, breathing proclamation of the gospel itself. His disclosure in v. 32 — “this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” — reveals that marriage was never merely about human beings. It was always a sign pointing beyond itself to the most magnificent love story in the universe. Every faithful Christian marriage is a living icon of the gospel.

The wife is called to submit (hypotassō — a voluntary, willing ordering, not forced compliance). This is not inferiority; the Son submits to the Father without being less than the Father (1 Cor. 11:3). It is a role, not a rank. What submission means: voluntarily honouring the husband’s leadership, bringing full voice and wisdom to the marriage, trusting the structure when decisions cannot be agreed. What it does not mean: blind obedience to sin (the limit is “as to the Lord”), enduring abuse, being silenced, or bearing a burden uniquely — the husband is called to die (v. 25), which by any honest measure is the greater weight. Submission is a gift freely given, not a cage imposed.

The husband is called to love (agapaō) his wife as Christ loved the church — and the standard is Calvary. Headship is servant-leadership, cross-shaped from the start. It means taking ultimate responsibility (God came looking for Adam first, Gen. 3:9), initiating love rather than waiting for it (Rom. 5:8), leading the household spiritually, and making decisions that bear the cost for her sake. What it does not mean: unilateral autocracy, spiritual superiority, overriding Scripture, silencing his wife, or a position of comfort. The head goes first into difficulty. “Not a crown to be claimed but a cross to be carried.”

The purpose of this love is the wife’s sanctification and eventual glorification (vv. 26–27) — the husband investing in her holiness through word, prayer, and attentive presence; holding before her a truer picture of who she is in Christ than the voices she grew up with. The one-flesh reality of v. 31 deepens this: what is done to her is done to him. Her flourishing is inseparable from his own — so he attends to her the way he attends to pain in his own body: promptly, because she is part of him.

“One flesh” means a comprehensive, covenantal union: physical (sexual union as covenant sign), relational (lives genuinely intertwined, interests no longer separable), covenantal (permanent, witnessed by God, Mal. 2:14), and exclusive (one man, one woman, one union). What it does not mean: the loss of individual identity, perfect harmony without conflict, the superseding of all other relationships, or a reality achieved instantly. The leaving and the holding-fast of Gen. 2:24 are active and ongoing: a daily re-election of the spouse above all others.

The section closes with the double summary of v. 33: the husband loves, the wife respects. These are not identical but complementary — each addressed at the point of their deepest calling and their deepest vulnerability. And each is a daily practice long before it is a feeling: the husband who consistently turns toward his wife’s need, and the wife who consistently honours her husband’s leadership, are enacting the gospel in the most ordinary moments of married life — and the watching world sees something it cannot produce on its own.

The household code tradition (Haustafeln): Paul engages a well-established literary genre — Aristotle, the Stoics, Hellenistic Jewish writers all taught household management through three pairs: husband/wife, parent/child, master/slave. Paul uses the same structure but transforms it radically: he addresses the subordinate party first (giving them full moral standing as agents accountable to Christ); grounds every command in Christ rather than nature or social utility; gives the longer and more demanding command to the dominant party; and embeds the entire code in mutual submission (v. 21). The form is conventional; the content is a quiet revolution.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over His church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: "as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who "came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to "submit to your own husband, as to the Lord" (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb “submit” is not present in the Greek of v. 22 — it carries over from the mutual submission of v. 21. Wives are called to the same posture Paul has just called every believer to adopt toward one another, applied in the specific relation to their own husbands. “As to the Lord” — not because the husband is divine, but because the wife’s submission is ultimately an act of obedience to Christ who has ordered marriage this way. The husband’s authority is borrowed and bounded; the wife’s submission is given to God himself through this divinely appointed structure.

What submission means. The Greek hypotassō was a military term: to arrange oneself under the authority of another, to recognise an ordering. It is a voluntary, willing act — not forced compliance but a free choice to honour the structure God has established. Paul is not speaking of worth or intelligence or spiritual standing — Galatians 3:28 is clear that in Christ there is neither male nor female in terms of standing before God. He is speaking of role within the covenant of marriage, just as within the Trinity the Son submits to the Father without being in any way inferior to him (1 Cor. 11:3; 15:28). The pattern of submission within equality is written into the very life of God.

Submission in marriage means the wife voluntarily honours her husband’s God-given leadership role — supporting his decisions, deferring to his direction in the ordering of the household, and doing so not grudgingly but as a gift freely given. It is a posture of trust, not of passivity. The submitted wife is not a silent, opinionless presence; she brings her full wisdom, gifts, and voice to the marriage, and a good husband depends on that. But when decisions must be made and agreement cannot be reached, she trusts the structure God has given rather than insisting on her own way.

What submission does not mean. Paul is careful, and so must the preacher be:
